en: The Ratnaketudhāraṇī Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñāmitra of India during the Tang Dynasty.
Chapter One: Subduing Māra. Subduing Māra, Chapter One.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling at Rājagṛha, by the side of the Kalandaka Pond in the Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and were all possessed of right knowledge and well-liberated minds—as well as ten thousand great bodhisattvas, whose names were as follows:

Led by the youthful Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta—namely, the youthful Sumerukūṭa, Jñānodaka, Pṛthivījñāna, Vijayajñāna, Ākāśajñāna, Prajñājñāna, Vidyujjñāna, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, Abhibhūvijaya, Varuṇa, Vimala, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya—they were all preeminent. They had all attained the kṣānti-dhāraṇī-samādhi and were fully endowed with unobstructed wisdom regarding all phenomena. Their minds were impartial toward all sentient beings, they had transcended all realms of Māra, and they had skillfully entered the sphere of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas. Being fully possessed of great loving-kindness and great compassion, and being skilled in the wisdom of expedient means, they all dwelt with the Buddha at the Bamboo Grove, by the side of the Kalandaka Pond in the great city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there were two non-Buddhist practitioners who were wise, discerning, and proficient in more than eighteen branches of knowledge. Accompanied by five hundred followers, with one named Upatiṣya and the other named Kolita as their leaders, they spoke together in mutual agreement upon the nectar of the Dharma.
At that time, the Elder Aśvajit (translated into Chinese as Mashiang) dressed in his robes and took up his bowl during the first part of the day, entering the great city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.
When Upatiṣya saw Aśvajit, he was struck with wonder, thinking:
"I have never before seen a śramaṇa with such dignified and composed deportment; there is no one else who can equal this bhikṣu!"
I should go and ask: whom does this elder take as his teacher?
Under whom has he gone forth?
Upon whom does he rely to seek the Dharma?
At that time, Upatiṣya went to where he was, and having arrived, he exchanged greetings with him. After conversing on various matters, he stood to one side and addressed the Elder Aśvajit, saying:
"Whom do you take as your teacher?"
"Under whom did you go forth?
Under whom do you seek the Dharma?
At that time, the Elder Āśvajit replied to Upatiṣya:
“There is a son of the Śākya clan who is courageous and diligent, capable of great asceticism, and supremely sovereign in all respects.

Having already crossed the boundless great ocean of birth and death, he now desires to deliver sentient beings through his great compassion; he is named Buddha. He awakens sentient beings and dries up the ocean of suffering, being without equal. I constantly take refuge in him, seeking the stainless Dharma.”
Upatiṣya said: "What kind of Dharma does that teacher preach to you?
By what means does he instruct?"
Then, the Elder Āśvajit replied to Upatiṣya:
"Excellent! How wonderful!"
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
I shall speak for you.
Then he spoke these verses:
"Through the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma, the world thus revolves;
that afflictions and karma do not arise—this is what the Teacher has taught."
"Birth, old age, and death are certain to perish; that liberation is unsurpassed.
Like a courageous bull-king, the Tathāgata has realized this for himself and proclaimed it.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, Upatiṣya’s eye of Dharma became pure, free from dust and defilement; he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna and spoke this verse:
"I have realized and understood the true Dharma, forever drying up the river of birth and death;
that which the Tathāgata has spoken is a treasury of nectar difficult to obtain.
Sentient beings find relief from suffering, for wisdom is able to sever it."
"By practicing the various dharmas in their manifold ways, one can accomplish the ultimate path;
by walking this ultimate path, one attains peerless nirvāṇa.
At that time, having spoken this verse, Upatiṣya addressed the Elder Aśvajit, saying:
"Elder! Where is your teacher—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—now residing?
Aśvajit replied:

"Elder! My Teacher, the Tathāgata, is currently at the Kalandaka Pond in the Bamboo Grove near Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus who were originally followers of external paths and have now left the household life upon encountering the Buddha."
Upatiṣya said, "I shall now take leave of my spiritual friend and his retinue to go to the Buddha and renounce the household life.
At that time, Upatiṣya prostrated at the feet of Aśvajit, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having taken his leave, departed for the place where Kolita was.
At that time, Kutadanta saw Upatissa approaching from afar; having seen him, he said to Upatissa:
"Venerable sir!
Your faculties are pure and your countenance is serene; you must have attained the Deathless."
Upatiṣya said: "So it is, Elder!
I have now attained the Dharma of the Deathless."
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
I shall now explain for you the Dharma that I have attained.
At that time, Kūṭadanta rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and spoke this verse by way of request:
"Speak this auspicious path free from sorrow, This path that swiftly crosses the ocean of the three realms;
It discerns the great enemy thieves of the aggregates (skandhas); Having mounted this path, one shall not return again."
At that time, Upatiṣya recited the verses he had heard:
"By the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma, the world thus revolves;
When afflictions and karma do not arise, so says the Teacher."
"Birth, old age, and death are certain to perish; that liberation is unsurpassed.
Like that brave king of bulls, the Tathāgata has realized it for himself and speaks of it.
At that time, having heard this verse, Kūṭadanta was filled with great joy and once again praised him, requesting that he further explain the previous verse:
"The cessation of suffering is peaceful and stainless; the Muni has taught this Dharma.
All afflictions are extinguished, and all views and ignorance are severed.
Defiled conditioned things are empty, selfless, and not to be relied upon."
"Repeating the stainless verses, I have heard that one attains Nirvana.
At that time, Upatiṣya immediately repeated the verse he had heard:
"By the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma, the world thus revolves."
Defiled karma does not arise; thus has the Teacher spoken.
Birth, old age, and death are certain to perish; that liberation is unsurpassed.
Like a brave bull-king, the Tathāgata has realized it for himself and proclaimed it.

At that time, having heard these verses, Kūṭadanta was freed from dust and defilement; his Dharma-eye became pure, and he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. He then praised [the Buddha] with a verse:
“This true practice of the Dharma is a swift boat for crossing the stream;
this wisdom stills the three sufferings and is able to deliver one from the world.”
"The various aggregates and the demon of afflictions—knowing these, one can subdue them;
thus liberated and free from enmity and strife, one dries up the ocean of suffering.
At that time, Kutidva said:
"Where does the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
currently reside? Upatiṣya replied,
"Venerable sir!"

I have heard that the World-Honored One is currently at the Bamboo Grove, by the Kalandaka Pond in the great city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a multitude of bodhisattvas. I shall now certainly go with you to the place where the World-Honored One is, to seek ordination as a monk under the Buddha.
Kūṭadanta said: "So be it, Elder!
You may tell your disciples to go to the Blessed One and follow him forth into homelessness together."
Then Upatiṣya and Kolita went to their own assembly.

At that moment, in a single instant, Māra the Evil One heard that in the central kingdom of Magadha there were two non-Buddhist practitioners, Upatiṣya together with Kolita and their followers, who were wise, endowed with full renown, and far-famed as virtuous men, and that they intended to go forth and train in the path within the Dharma of the Śramaṇa Gautama.
He thought to himself: "Aha!
How marvelous!"

If these two men were to go forth as monastics within the Dharma of that śramaṇa Gautama, they would empty my domain; I should go to those two great men and destroy their renunciation, causing them to adhere to evil views.

At that moment, the Evil Māra, in a single thought-instant, vanished from his own palace and assumed the appearance, form, and deportment of Āśvajit. He then appeared before the two men along the way and spoke these words:
"As I previously declared, your testing was not definitive;
according to what you intend to do, you should quickly enjoy sensual pleasures."
All karma, whether black or white, lacks both cause and effect;
there is no birth, aging, sickness, or death, nor is there a future world.
Regarding the karma of merit and non-merit, there is no such causal action that produces them.
"The son of the Śākyas speaks for his own profit; do not believe him and depart.
At that time, having heard these words, Upatiṣya and Kolita both thought to themselves:
"This evil Māra has come, wishing to destroy our undertaking of the homeless life."
At that time, Upatiṣya looked back at his disciples and spoke these words:
"You all should now call to mind all the faults and afflictions of the world."
He then spoke this verse:
“Sentient beings are oppressed by old age And entangled by the suffering of death;
One should sever both of these And resolutely go forth into homelessness.”
At that time, Kutadanta replied to the Māra in verse:
"Knowing the unsurpassed, wholesome wisdom, And upholding the Dharma to extinguish the three sufferings—
Though you speak of not severing greed, My wisdom remains forever unshaken."
Such a firm resolve as this does not exist in others.
Having emerged from the wheel of suffering and being undeluded by right knowledge,
do not assume the likeness of a lion while uttering the cry of a jackal.
At that time, the gods who had realized the truths, dwelling in the midst of the sky, praised the two men, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You two, O great men, are the foremost among all sentient beings; this path is sublime and most excellent, being the very first in all the world."
This path brings rest to all suffering; this path enters the sphere of activity of all Tathāgatas; this path is praised by all Buddhas, namely, the renunciation of the Buddha.
At that time, Māra, his heart filled with grief and suffering, vanished and disappeared.
Then Upatiṣya and Kolita, observing their own assembly, called to their disciples and spoke these words:
"You should know that we wish to cross the ocean of suffering of old age and death; therefore, we have gone forth as monastics under the Buddha."
"You all! If you do not delight in the Buddha’s going forth, you may remain here.
At that time, the five hundred disciples all spoke these words:

“We understand that all who comprehend the Dharma do so by training under a teacher. Since both our teachers have resolutely gone forth into homelessness at a great monastery, and since that is the place where our teachers relied for their renunciation, we shall follow our teachers and likewise go forth into homelessness to study the Path within that community.”
At that time, Upatiṣya and Kolita, together with their five hundred followers, were about to go to where the Buddha was.

Then, the Evil Māra, having learned of their intention, manifested a great pit outside the city of Rājagṛha, one hundred yojanas deep, so as to prevent those two men from reaching the presence of the World-Honored One, the Buddha.
At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Tathāgata caused those two men not to see the great pit, so that they proceeded directly along the path.
Then, before the two men, the evil Māra again manifested a high and precipitous mountain, a thousand yojanas in height, steep, rugged, and solid, without any cracks or openings.
Upon that mountain, he further manifested a thousand lions, fierce and terrifying.

At that time, through the power of his supernormal faculties, the World-Honored One empowered those two men so that they no longer saw the great mountain or the lions, nor did they hear any fierce or terrifying sounds; they proceeded directly to where the World-Honored One was, to the place where he sat surrounded and honored by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands, as he preached the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see those two virtuous men, leaders among the assembly, who have come to me together with their retinues?"
“Do you see them?
The bhikṣus replied,
“We all say that we see them.”
The Buddha said:

“These good men and their followers have gone forth from my presence; one among them shall be the foremost in wisdom among all my śrāvaka disciples, and another shall be the foremost in supernormal powers among my assembly of śrāvakas.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly who praised them with a verse:
“These two wise ones, together with their retinue, The Supreme Benefactor has already prophesied;
Possessing wisdom, supernormal powers, and fearlessness, Therefore I welcome these two Great Men.”

At that time, having spoken these verses, the bhikṣu rose from his seat and, together with an immeasurable assembly of bhikṣus, as well as laymen and laywomen who had gone forth, went out to meet those two men and greeted them with kind words.

Then those two men went to where the Buddha was; having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, stood before him, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"We now seek to leave the household life under the Buddha, receive the bhikṣu precepts, and practice the holy life.
The Buddha said,
"Good sons!..."
"What are the names of you two?
Upatiṣya replied, "Tiṣya is my father's name and Śāri is my mother's name; because I am named after my mother, I am called Śāriputra."
"My parents have now granted me permission to leave the household life. Kūṭadanta said:
"Kauṇḍinya is your father and Moggalāna is your mother; because I was born from my mother, I am named Moggalāna."
"Our parents have now granted us permission to leave the household life.
The Buddha said,
"You two, along with your kinsmen and retinues, may go forth under me and fully practice the holy life."
When these words had been spoken, those two individuals attained full ordination; and before long, the assembly of five hundred followers likewise attained full ordination under their two teachers.
At that time, Māra immediately transformed himself into the likeness of Maheśvara, stood before the Buddha, and spoke these verses:

“Those in the world with sharp intelligence who engage in debate, And those with superior wisdom in skillful means who have reached the other shore— They all come to prostrate to me; I am their great teacher.”
The disciples of Gautama, together with their retinues, all should quickly take refuge in me;
I shall now extensively expound for you the path that is peaceful, quiescent, and sublime.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“The path you speak of leads to evil realms; Sentient beings who travel it sink into the sea of suffering.
My path can cause both the moving and the unmoving To completely dry up the sea of worldly suffering.”
Why do you act with such arrogance, impudence, and shamelessness, further raising the cry of a haughty jackal?
I shall now repel and destroy your demonic deeds; they shall no longer have power over me.
At that time, Māra transformed himself into the likeness of Maheśvara, then vanished and disappeared.
He then assumed the form of Brahmā, Śakra, the King of Devas, and stood before the Buddha, reciting these verses:
"The sprouts of afflictions, karma, and existence Have already been severed by wisdom."
Why exert yourself so strenuously here to labor for the benefit of sentient beings?
You have no mastery over the world, and they lack the capacity to be vessels for the Path.
O Muni, your illness has already been cured; it is fitting that you enter Nirvana swiftly.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Māra King with these verses:
“I observe all sentient beings, More numerous than the sands of the Ganges;
By the power of great compassion, I teach and transform them to bring about their liberation.”
I shall bring liberation to beings of high, middle, and low station throughout the world;
once all beings are liberated, only then will I enter nirvana.
Why, then, with such malicious intent, do you deceitfully and sycophantically entreat me?
At that time, Māra the Evil One felt regret and sorrow in his heart; he vanished before the Buddha and returned to his own celestial palace, where he entered the Chamber of Sorrow and sat in silence.
At that moment, in a single kṣaṇa, Māra’s retinue questioned one another:
"For what reason has our Great King entered the chamber of sorrow and distress, such that no one knows?"

At that time, the five hundred celestial maidens of Māra, adorned in various ornaments and each holding flower garlands, powdered incense, and unguents, played five hundred kinds of divine musical instruments with the most exquisite singing, dancing, and performance, gathering before the King of Māra in a manner most delightful to behold.
At that time, the Māra wept piteously; grasping his hands together, he suppressed his cries of grief. Having done this, he remained silent for a moment.
The female dancers then began to sing and dance once more, assuming joyful expressions to gladden the Māra.
At that time, the Māra raised his hand and cried out loudly, saying these words:
"Silence! Silence!"
This continued up to seven times, yet the female musicians remained silent.
At that time, there was a courtesan in the palace of Māra named Vidyutmanojñaruta; she approached the King of Māra, bowed with palms joined, and spoke these verses:
"You now dwell in sovereignty, yet you look upon the signs of death with anxiety;
because you carry this heavy burden, you have now become terrified.
Who is there among your powerful enemies that would cause you such grief and lack of joy?"
At that time, Māra replied with a verse:
“I have a great enemy who has subdued his mind; The son of Śākya, well-trained in illusory arts, I have no skillful means to destroy him;
In this way, before long, the realm of desire shall be empty.”
Then, that courtesan spoke in verse:
"The Great Master’s skillful means are truly immeasurable; Through diligent effort, he will surely destroy him without remainder.
Who can untie the long-lasting bonds of the three realms? Who can exhaust the ocean in which one is submerged by craving?"
At that time, the Māra replied with a verse:
“Generosity and ascetic practices, With compassion and vows as his snares,
He holds the bow of emptiness and signlessness— The foremost among all weapons.”
Able to sever birth and death, with all states of existence exhausted without remainder;
taking emptiness as their city and grove, these disciples dwell among the mountain valleys.
Diligently and constantly practicing meditative concentration, they exhaust all faults and afflictions of existence.
Through the power of skillful means and supernormal knowledge, with compassion as his companion and aid,
the Muni has completely subdued Upagupta and others;
within those three realms, he skillfully disciplines and guides them through skillful means.
"I wish to empty my realm, leaving nothing behind at all.

At that time, the five hundred female musicians, having heard from the Māra king the praise of all the Tathāgata’s merits, immediately attained a bodhisattva samādhi called "The Lightning Flash Samādhi that is Free from All Marks."

At that time, those five hundred female musicians immediately took various celestial ornaments, rained down heavenly incense, flowers, and celestial music, and from afar toward the place where the Buddha was, made offerings to the World-Honored One.

Upon the bamboo grove, it was as if rain were falling; because they had received the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s supernormal power, those goddesses saw the World-Honored One and his assembly from afar. Having seen them, they rejoiced, giving rise to pure faith and the highest reverence.
At that time, the bhikṣus among the assembly, seeing such signs within the bamboo grove, were struck with doubt and wonder, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"We have never before seen or heard of such auspicious signs as this rain of fragrant flowers and the like within the Bamboo Grove; could it be that Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others are manifesting these portents?"
"For what cause and condition do we behold such a rare wonder?
At that time, the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:

"It is not these two who are manifesting supernatural signs; rather, these are five hundred celestial maidens of Māra from his palace, raining down these fragrant flowers and ornaments as an offering to me."
"Before long they will come here, and all shall receive from me the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the five hundred female attendants of the Māra King heard the Buddha’s prediction from afar; their joy increased further and they gave rise to pure faith. Because of this pure faith, they immediately attained the *samādhi* of the non-forgetfulness of the bodhicitta.

At that time, the five hundred female attendants of Māra, having draped their robes over one shoulder and knelt with their right knees upon the ground, joined their palms in reverence toward the direction of the Buddha within the palace of Māra and spoke these verses:
"All the world is blind and without eyes; Only the Buddha, the One Man, is called the Seer.
He can dry up the river of craving of humans and devas; The Tathāgata has delivered himself and all others."
"How may we quickly attain Buddhahood, becoming those who can preach the Dharma and are revered by humans and devas?
This female body is loathsome and should be abandoned; let us quickly approach the Muni to hear the True Dharma.
May the Tathāgata, with his supreme supernormal wisdom, reveal it to us and act as our supreme guide."
Holding those jewels of the unsurpassed factors of enlightenment, with stainless and wondrous speech like a pure lamp,
possessing peerless and supreme power to subdue Māra— awaken us and grant us our prophecy!
At that time, five hundred celestial maidens of Māra’s palace rose from their seats, approached the place where the Māra-king was, and with one voice and in unison, spoke this verse:
“The Tathāgata’s supreme virtues are forever unmoving; how could you give rise to anger toward the Buddha?”
This body is oppressed by manifold sufferings, yet it further gives rise to intoxication and pride, smearing itself with defilement;
one should abandon this anger and cultivate resolute faith, pulling others out from the mud of birth-and-death and arrogance.
The essential nature of sentient beings is known by the Buddha; we should go to the presence of his compassion.
At that time, Māra the King thought of those women and gave rise to such an intense and evil intention:
"I should now bind these five hundred courtesans with five kinds of fetters, causing them to remain here and not go to the Buddha's side."
Because these five hundred women had obtained the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s power of mindfulness, they could not be restrained by that Māra-king.
At that time, the five hundred courtesans set out from that palace of Māra to go to the presence of the Buddha.
As he was about to set out, Māra became deeply resentful and thought to himself:
"I shall now use the power of my own realm to restrain these women.

He immediately raised a tempestuous Vairambha wind out of season that filled the void of space, intending to cause the women to lose their sense of direction so that they would return to his palace and no longer see Gautama.
By the power of the Buddha, not even a subtle breeze could arise, nor could a single hair-tip be moved, let alone anything immeasurable.
At that time, Māra’s sorrow and suffering increased further; his heart was filled with remorse and anguish, and he wept aloud, calling to his sons and their retinues.
A great sound filled all the palaces of Māra, and he spoke these verses:
"The beloved sons and retinue have all assembled; My heart is tormented by distress like a tree of poison.
He has destroyed the power of my supernatural realm; The Lion of the Śākyas with his sweet words, flattery, and illusions."
At that time, all the sons and daughters of Māra, along with their retinues, hearing this sound, rushed forth and stood before Māra.
Among those followers was a son of Māra named Vijñāna, who stood with palms joined and spoke these verses:
"This is not the conflagration at the end of an eon, nor is it a sign of death; why, then, do you give rise to such various anxieties and distress?"
"He possesses no great power to overcome his enemies; why does he, with such extraordinary wisdom, appear like one who is deluded?
At that time, the Māra King replied in verse:
"This son of the Śākyas now sits beneath a tree in that forest."
A great enemy stands before me; how can you say there is none?
His deceit possesses superior power, causing my heart to be wild with fear;
my army and my sons are like charcoal cast into a blazing fire.
The one renowned as the Supreme Person, wise and possessed of many arts—
whether already assembled or yet to be assembled— I now take refuge in him all together.
My enemy, feigning intimacy with deceit, contends with great skill and power.
Even those of high renown and supreme wisdom are all pulled by the hook of the Dharma.
Now these female attendants have no compassion for me;
seeing that I have abandoned what they once loved, they have all gone to where the śramaṇa is.
Pointing to me as his witness, today I take refuge in him;
throughout all the realms of the three existences, he causes all guile and illusion to become void.
Though he possesses great power, I shall shatter it until it is reduced to ashes.
"We, the entire host, should diligently perform what must be done.
At that time, all the sons of Māra, together with all their internal and external retinues, joined their palms and spoke thus:

"We shall all prepare our chariots and empower ourselves with supernatural powers; we will manifest this realm to him so that he may know it, and cause that son of the Śākyas to retreat and be crushed like ashes."
"If we should prevail, it would be well for us; if we do not prevail, we shall take refuge in him.

In the past, when we approached the Bodhi tree surrounded by a great army, we beheld the son of the Śākyas alone and without a companion; yet by his supernatural power, our entire host was utterly defeated and dispersed. How much more so now, when he has achieved success with an immeasurable multitude of followers?"
Then Māra replied,
"Go for now, my sons!
You must return only when you have been able to slay that śramaṇa Gautama."
"If you are unable [to do so], you must likewise return to your palace and guard it yourself.

At that time, Māra immediately deployed his left and right hosts, numbering one hundred and twenty thousand, extending even beyond that count to eighty-four thousand *yojanas*, until all the military forces were completely filled [the space]. Furthermore, by the power of his swift supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), he manifested a great black wind, blew forth great black clouds, and rained down great torches of fire, which completely filled all four continents.
Again, he struck Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, with his hand, causing all four continents to tremble.
He further let out a most evil and terrifying sound, by which Mount Sumeru, the kings of all other mountains, the great earth, its peaks, and stones were all shaken with alarm.

By this shock, the small and large ponds, rivers, and the waters of the great ocean all became surging with waves; seeing this, all the nāgas, mahānāgas, yakṣas, and mahāyakṣas leaped up into the air.

These hosts of Māras, dwelling on the summit of Mount Sumeru, further hurled great boulders the size of a yojana; amidst this, the land of Magadha was struck and shaken like a great torrential rainstorm.

Furthermore, they rained down swords, pestles, clubs, spears, great stones, crescent-headed blades, curved lances, short halberds, iron-handled tiger-toothed maces, and great crescent-headed arrows, falling like rain.

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately entered the samādhi called "Crushing the Battlefield of Māra. All weapons and great blazing fires in the void were transformed into a rain of flowers—namely, a rain of *utpala* flowers, a rain of *padma* flowers, a rain of *kumuda* flowers, a rain of *puṇḍarīka* flowers, a rain of *māndārava* flowers, and a rain of *mahāmāndārava* flowers.

In the rain, the terrifying and agitating sounds that had arisen in the kingdom of Magadha were transformed into various subtle and exquisite sounds, namely: the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, the sound of the Saṅgha, the sound of the pāramitās, the sound of the supernormal powers, the sound of non-retrogression, the sound of receiving empowerment, the sound of the four māras being defeated, the sound of proceeding to the site of enlightenment, and even the sounds of grasping and non-grasping.
Furthermore, he transformed the entire great earth of these four continents, such that all medicinal herbs, forests, mountains, rocks, and soil became the seven treasures.
At that time, there was no wind or dust in the world; everything was tranquil and still.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested his physical form, exercising sovereign mastery beyond the Brahma-world. From each of the marks upon his body, up to the mark of the invisible crown of the head, he emitted great radiance that illuminated the trichiliocosm, pervading it all with brilliant light.

At that time, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—along with those in the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama—all throughout this trichiliocosm, beheld the World-Honored One and his great radiance.

At that time, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues, came from both the earth and the sky to the place where the Buddha was. They scattered flowers as an offering; having arrived, they circumambulated him to the right, praised him, and prostrated.

At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of beings from the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama each recalled their previously planted roots of goodness, called out "Namo Buddhāya," and upon the conclusion of their existence in the evil destinies, were reborn in the heavens.

At that time, the twenty-two thousand sons of Māra, together with their retinues, having witnessed such miraculous transformations of the Buddha, each conceived a rare faith toward the Buddha. Together with those five hundred celestial maidens of Māra, they prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, joined their palms in reverence, and praised him with these verses:
“Your wondrous form and pure body reflect the ocean of wisdom; Your fame is lofty and far-reaching, reaching everywhere.
With a golden radiance like Mount Sumeru, We, who have no other protector, take refuge in you.”
Sentient beings have lost their way and none can see it; The Tathāgata’s sun of wisdom shines upon it clearly.
He nurtures and protects sentient beings, never retreating; As our close guide, we take refuge in him.
Accumulating a treasury of wisdom, immeasurably rich; The nature of his mind is liberated like space;
Moistening with compassion, he teaches according to capacities; All that is accomplished—I take refuge in him.
The wilderness of birth and death is difficult to cross; the Tathāgata can reveal the path of liberation.
Skillfully explaining cause and effect, he brings them to clear understanding; abiding in supreme compassion, I take refuge in him.
Sense objects are like illusions, mirages, and the moon reflected in water; obscured by the darkness of ignorance, beings cling to various desires.
The Buddha, as the King of Physicians, rescues the world; therefore, we take refuge in him.
The Buddha is the true bridge of Dharma that crosses the four floods; Rich in the seven treasures, he constantly provides for all.
The World-Honored One reveals the Right Path to the world; To this Great Compassionate Father, I should offer worship.
We have harbored evil intentions toward the Tathāgata; we now repent before the Supreme Awakened One.
May all our evils be forever severed; may the Buddha accept us as his supreme refuge.
We all renounce the factions of Māra and together resolve upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta;
we universally exhort all classes of sentient beings until the great vow of awakening reaches its ultimate limit, leaving none behind.

The Buddha can reveal my supreme practice; the pāramitās that I have practiced are exactly as the Tathāgata has taught, without any discrepancy. How many dharmas must be fully perfected to reach bodhi?
The flowers scattered upon the Buddha form a floral canopy, manifesting infinite buddha-fields;
I now prostrate to the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings, and pray for the bliss of nirvana to benefit the world.

At that time, all the retinues of Māra, together with the celestial maidens of Māra, each took heavenly flowers and scattered them from afar over the Buddha. Through the empowerment of the World-Honored One’s supernatural power, these were transformed into flower canopies that completely covered the immeasurable koṭis, nayutas, hundreds of thousands of Ganges-sand numbers of Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.

Beyond that number, they transformed into flower canopies that completely covered all the Buddhas currently present throughout the ten directions, hovering in the void close above the crowns of those Buddhas' heads.

At that time, the five hundred courtesans of that Māra king, along with their retinues, all beheld the infinite, incalculable Buddha-fields of the ten directions where the Buddhas were teaching the Dharma in peace; they also saw those Buddhas surrounded by their assemblies, seated with subtle and majestic deportment of blazing intensity, and they saw the flower canopies abiding in the sky above, closely covering the crowns of the Buddhas' heads.

All those various Buddhas are of one and the same color, and their manifested physical forms and characteristics are entirely identical; it is only that the World-Honored One, seated upon his lion throne, appears different due to the various adornments of his retinue and merits.

Furthermore, they heard the Buddhas’ voices teaching the Dharma through phrases and meanings that pervade all places; because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had bestowed his mindful empowerment upon them, these demonic followers were able to witness such supernatural transformations.
Having seen this, they conceived supreme delight and pure faith; prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, they sat before him to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, all the sons of Māra, together with their retinue of twelve *bimbara* [trillion], returned to the palace of Māra and said to him:
"We have committed such extensive evil deeds, yet we were not even able to destroy a single pore of Gautama."
At that time, furthermore, twenty thousand māras took refuge in the Tathāgata and listened to the Dharma before the Buddha.
Then, having lost his majestic power, the Māra King became greatly enraged and spoke these words:
"Today I have no other thought than this: I shall not be able to slay the son born of the Śākya clan and cause him to perish."
"What is this dwelling?
he asked, and then returned to the palace of Māra, entered the chamber of sorrow and affliction, and sat there in silence.
*Ratnaketudhāraṇī Sūtra*, Fascicle One.
The Ratnaketudhāraṇī Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Prajñāmitra of India during the Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Two: The Account of Past Events (Pūrvayoga). Chapter Two: The Account of Past Events.
Then the celestial maidens of Māra, the sons of Māra, and their retinues addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, Blessed One!
We now aspire to seek such signs, such vehicles, such eloquence and wisdom, and such supernormal powers, great compassion, and skillful means.”
How rare, Blessed One!
You are fully endowed with such dharmas as wisdom, skillful means, and supernormal powers, O Blessed One!
“By being endowed with how many dharmas can a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from evil friends and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can possess four dharmas, they will distance themselves from evil friends and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are these four?
First is non-appropriation, second is non-explanation, third is non-seeing, and fourth is emptiness without discrimination.
"Good son! What is meant by non-appropriation?

This means not grasping at any phenomena; there is not a single phenomenon that can be obtained. One neither accepts nor rejects, neither affirms nor denies, neither establishes nor clings to, and neither discriminates nor fails to discriminate.

This means that when practicing the *dānapāramitā*, one does not grasp at the fruit of the *dānapāramitā*; one neither accepts nor rejects, neither affirms nor denies, neither establishes nor clings to, and neither discriminates nor fails to discriminate. This applies even up to the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is likewise neither discrimination nor non-discrimination.
"Furthermore, good son! What is it that is not taught? It is said:

one does not teach that a sentient being can be apprehended; one does not teach a life-principle, nor a soul, nor a person; one does not teach that a realm of sentient beings can be apprehended; one does not teach that there is a mind that grasps at anything; and so on, up to: neither conceptualizing nor non-conceptualizing."
"Furthermore, good son!
What is meant by 'not seeing'?

It refers to not seeing form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena; not grasping at form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena; and even not conceptualizing them, nor not conceptualizing them."
"Furthermore, good son!
What is emptiness without discrimination?

It refers to all phenomena that are objects of perception—the causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases throughout the three times and the triple world—which neither arise nor rely [on anything], which have no characteristic of birth, and which are neither grasped nor discarded, even to the point of neither discriminating nor not discriminating."

Why is this? Because one has abandoned all formations (*saṃskāra*), all graspings (*upādāna*), and all bodies, as well as both conceptualization and non-conceptualization; because the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) cannot be apprehended [as a separate entity], one should practice in this manner.

Why is this so? Good son! All phenomena and all-knowledge—even unto being without sound, without mark, without letter, and without vow; without arising and without cessation, without essence and without attachment, without object and without self; invisible and quiescent; free from marks, free from thought, and free from extinction; without darkness and without light, without location and without sphere; without root and without companion; inconceivable and immeasurable; without greed and without stinginess, without practice and without speech; without depth and without shallowness, without reception and without reliance; without consciousness, without grasping, without shadow, and not for even a single moment; without limits and without anything at all—ultimately, there is nothing whatsoever.

Why is this? Because all-knowledge and so forth are like space; since a correspondence cannot be apprehended, one does not establish a correspondence, does not grasp a correspondence, and does not engage in a correspondence. Whether in correspondence or non-correspondence, one neither discriminates nor does not discriminate; one should practice in this manner.
“Good son! These are called the four dharmas which, when fully possessed, enable a bodhisattva mahāsattva to remain far removed from evil friends and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Good son!

Regarding all internal and external objects, if one uses the wisdom of omniscience to observe, investigate, and establish their basis and formation, yet clings to these two marks and discriminates them with the mind, thereby giving rise to dualistic attachment, one will then be far removed from omniscience."
What are the two characteristics?
If one observes the sense bases (*āyatana*) and so forth, and grasps at or establishes these two characteristics, this is called being far removed from omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
If one grasps at or establishes the practice and its fruit, these are the two types of conceptual discrimination.
To grasp at and establish signs regarding sentient beings constitutes dualistic discrimination.

To reveal and designate the path of speech, and to establish the dharmas of dhāraṇī and sound, while using wisdom to observe whether things are annihilated or eternal, also constitutes dualistic discrimination.
Sentient beings, life-span, nourishment, and the person (puruṣa) act as the basis for establishing the notion of an agent; these two are conceptual distinctions.
That which exists here or there, whether established through deliberation or not established through deliberation—these two are conceptual distinctions.

If one uses the wisdom of omniscience to observe the three periods of time and seeks out that which is produced by the "I" as the agent who accumulates karma, establishing and grasping at these two—the self and the action—these are dualistic discriminations.
If one possesses such dualistic discrimination, one will be unable to attain omniscience.

“Good son! It is as if one seeking fire in the cold were instead to take up earth; as if one seeking a drink in thirst were instead to take up fire; as if one seeking food in hunger were instead to take up stone; as if one seeking flowers for adornment were instead to take up clothing; as if one seeking fragrance for incense were instead to take up a corpse; as if one seeking clothes while traveling were instead to take up filth; as if one seeking fragrance for anointing were instead to take up empty space. Such it is, such it is!”
"Good son!

If one practices with attachment, observing this body through the two modes of grasping at signs and establishing them, yet seeks omniscience, one will merely waste one's diligence; there will be neither the Path nor its fruit."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva among the assembly named Dharimati. He rose from his seat, bowed with palms joined before the World-Honored One, and spoke these words: “Bhagavān!
"If a dharma is inexpressible, can one attain bodhi?
The Buddha said:
"You should now know that there is no attainment of bodhi, nor is there any bodhi that can be expressed."
"Good son! Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
Since you ask thus, speak as you please and according to your own inclination.
Does any thing whatsoever, or omniscience itself, possess an intrinsic nature, a characteristic mark, or a name?
The Bodhisattva Dharanidhara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“No, Bhagavan!”
If there is speech, one falls into the view of eternalism; if there is no speech, one falls into the view of nihilism—even the Middle Way cannot be apprehended therein.

It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither grasped nor clung to, neither arising nor perishing. It transcends incalculable, immeasurable, and innumerable aeons; it is without darkness and without light. To contemplate in this manner is to attain Bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Vidyudmati said: “Bhagavān!
One attains bodhi by thus knowing well that there is neither coming nor going, and by thus entering well into this.”
The Bodhisattva Vairocana said: "So it is, Bhagavān!

The Dharma is neither characterized by arrival nor by non-arrival; it is neither a time of attainment nor a time of non-attainment; it is neither realization nor non-realization; it is neither cessation nor non-cessation; it is neither the three times nor not the three times; it is neither the three vehicles nor not the three vehicles; furthermore, it cannot be obtained through the measurement of the accumulation of practices and vows."
"One who knows in this way shall attain bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha said, "Bhagavān!"

If all dharmas are neither the three realms nor the three fetters, neither the three insights nor the three vehicles, neither the aggregates, elements, nor sense bases; neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization;
neither decreasing nor increasing, and without any aggregation—having known them thus, one attains bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Vajramati said:

"The dharmas of ordinary beings and the dharmas of noble ones, the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training, the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—these are neither conceptualized nor non-conceptualized, and they cannot be known through synthesis or measurement.
One who knows them in this way attains bodhi."
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati said:
"Through the suchness of quiescence and the observation of suchness—neither abandoning nor dwelling—one attains bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi said:
"If all dharmas are unborn, unattainable, and timeless, being without the marks of conceptual discrimination, then one attains bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Acintyaprajñā said:
"If one uses the mind that observes the triple world to reckon its entry into the mind, this is called 'two minds'."
"When these two minds cannot be apprehended through such observation, it is by means of non-apprehension that one attains bodhi.
Bodhisattva Pratyāgamana said:

"If all dharmas are without attachment, without craving, without relinquishment, without obstruction, without aspiration, without delusion, without grasping, and without letting go, then one attains bodhi."
The Bodhisattva Padmagarbha said:

"If one realizes that the natures of both sin and merit equally enter into this Dharma, and through profound patience remains unattached to 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' neither conceptualizing nor non-conceptualizing—those who contemplate in this way shall attain bodhi."
The Bodhisattva Candraprabha said:
"If one contemplates all phenomena as gathering and dispersing according to conditions, devoid of intrinsic nature, like the moon reflected in water;
having understood them thus, one attains bodhi."
The Bodhisattva Gaganamati said:
"If one does not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding all dharmas— whether they possess darkness or light, arising or ceasing, increase or decrease—
and knows them in this way, one attains bodhi."
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said:
"If one cultivates the perfections (pāramitās) purified of the three spheres (trimaṇḍala), such that they are non-apprehendable, neither defiled nor non-defiled;
one who cultivates in this manner shall attain bodhi."
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"If one does not take as an object of perception nor receive the support of the triple world, nor the support of the Brahma-abodes, then one attains bodhi.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“Bhagavān! One who understands this single profound dharma-gate is neither stained nor unstained by any phenomena; that single dharma-gate is what is called ‘non-self.’”

Having realized that this single dharma is neither perceived nor observed, there is nothing to bring forth and nothing to send away; it cannot be gathered or dispersed, made bright or dark, born or extinguished, increased or diminished.

That which is to be liberated should not be defiled by turbidity, for it is free from discrimination. Through this single gateway of the dharma, by means of the wisdom of all-knowledge, one attains bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Huai-aile said:
"Mañjuśrī! Such a dharma-gate of omniscient wisdom entirely enters the profound realm of emptiness that accords with reality."
"For what purpose is there the performance of intentional acts and the practice of skillful means? Mañjuśrī replied:
"It is for the sake of abandoning evil views and practicing right view, without establishing them through delusion."
Abandoning a crooked mind and cultivating upright conduct, one does not engage in false establishment;
abandoning the ten unwholesome paths and revering the Triple Gem, one does not engage in false establishment;
speaking well, one does not engage in false establishment.
Right livelihood is not falsely established;
the relinquishing of all fetters is not falsely established;
great compassion that is impartial and does not abandon any sentient being is not falsely established.
The three protections: not falsely establishing [anything], for there is no dharma of falsehood or deception;
not falsely establishing [anything], for it is neither born nor extinguished;
protecting and upholding the True Dharma, without false establishment.
He relinquishes all possessions without false presumption;
he constantly provides assistance to sentient beings of little strength without false presumption;
and those who are terrified find refuge in him without false presumption.
To those who follow non-ways, he shows the right path, yet does not falsely establish it;
he practices patience and gentleness, yet does not falsely establish it;
he does not cling to any signs, yet does not falsely establish them.
He has abandoned all dust, defilements, darkness, and obscurations, and does not falsely establish them;
he has abandoned all dedication toward karmic rewards, and does not falsely establish them. "Good son!

These twenty kinds of skillful means can bring about the attainment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). All distinctions of written characters, sounds, speech, and the meanings of phrases are entirely suchness; this is called the skillful means for entering the knowledge of all modes.

All that is spoken by the Tathāgatas, as well as all that is spoken by other non-Buddhist paths—including all grasping and abandoning, arising and ceasing, and even the knowledge of the three gates of liberation—the dharmas of causes, conditions, karma, and practice, all enter into suchness (*tathatā*). One should know that these are all the skillful means of the wisdom of omniscient awakening.
The Bodhisattva Destroyer of Delight said: “So it is,
so it is, Mañjuśrī!”

For one who understands this profound dharma-gate, not a single dharma is to be perceived; there is neither the dharma taught, nor the teacher, and even the words, phrases, and meanings should all be relinquished.
"If there is no correspondence between practice and cognition, and all entries are likewise so, this is called the awakening-knowledge of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
Son of good family, you have skillfully expounded this single Dharma-gate; it is through the wisdom of all-knowledge that one attains this Dharma.
What is meant by "not falsely establishing all dharmas"?

It refers to not falsely establishing the limit of non-arising and non-perishing; not falsely establishing the limit of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; not falsely establishing the limit of space and nirvāṇa; and the limit of non-arising and non-explanation—even all dharmas are likewise thus.

He demonstrates to all sentient beings that all phenomena have no limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); he demonstrates that all objects of attachment, as well as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the three times and the three realms, are without any limit of existence; he enters the limit of emptiness of the three modes of action; he enters the limit of non-reality of the aggregates of phenomena, the aggregates of retribution, and the aggregates of aggregation and dispersion; he enters emptiness and the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). He fully possesses the meaning of all teachings on non-dharma; this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s entry into the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), and by means of this knowledge of all-knowledge, he receives his prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

When this Dharma was being taught, twenty thousand of Māra’s courtesans, along with the retinue of Māra’s sons, heard what the Buddha had said and simultaneously attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). They all abandoned all coarse activities of body and mind and attained the body born of its own nature (*svabhāva-ja-kāya*).

Furthermore, twenty-eight thousand sentient beings attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and nine million two hundred thousand devas and humans attained various bodhisattva samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.

At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others who had attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas rained down celestial flowers upon the Buddha; they fell in profusion, like a falling rain.
Prostrating with their heads to the ground, they bowed at the Buddha’s feet and spoke these words: “Bhagavān!

If we encounter unwholesome and evil friends, and through associating with the wicked we act freely in evil, we shall never, for even a single thought-moment, give rise to a wholesome mind toward the mass of all merits and roots of goodness belonging to all sentient beings.”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

In the past, throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, you have personally approached and made offerings to countless Buddhas. By virtue of these karmic conditions, you have now conceived a joyful devotion and have once again encountered a Buddha. Now, for the sake of severing the doubts of sentient beings, I shall explain to you the causal conditions of your past lives.”

“Good son! In the past, immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, there was a kalpa named Mahābalasampanna. In this Jambudvīpa, there was a wheel-turning king named Utpala; he possessed sovereign power and ruled over the four continents. Both the king and his ministers and subjects lived for sixty-eight thousand years.”

At that time, there was a Buddha in the world named Candraprabhāgandhavijaya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
"Although the sentient beings of that land dwell amidst the five turbidities, because they cultivate goodness, they are not defiled by the dharmas of desire.
At that time, that Buddha constantly expounds for the fourfold assembly the Dharma corresponding to the three vehicles."
At that time, King Utpala, having arrayed his fourfold army and accompanied by his consort, the ladies of the harem, and his retinue, went to where the Buddha Candraprabha was.

Upon arrival, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, scattered various flowers, burned various incenses, and performed many musical offerings. Having thus made offerings to the Buddha, he circumambulated him three times to the right, and further prostrated at the feet of the community of bhikṣus. Then, with these two verses, he praised and questioned the Buddha:
“O Greatly Meritorious One, looked up to by devas and nāgas, O Unsurpassed Honored One, who has forever severed all afflictions, ... (the rest of the verse follows).”
Using the seven treasures of Dharma to benefit the world, pray tell, what kind of wondrous wisdom have you attained?
Acting as a lamp of great compassion to extinguish the darkness of the world, you subdue the sorrows of birth, old age, and death;
able to block the three evil realms for humans and devas, what Dharma do you teach to liberate beings from the path of Māra?
"Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata Candraprabhā-gandhavijaya addressed King Utpala, saying:
'Great King!'"
By being endowed with three dharmas, one can attain the subtle and wondrous wisdom of a bodhisattva.
What are these three?
First, great compassion like that of a mother, which can serve as the ultimate place of reliance for all sentient beings;
Second, through diligent and tireless effort, one is able to extinguish all the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings;
third, one contemplates all phenomena with equanimity, seeing that they are devoid of a life-principle, devoid of a nourisher, devoid of a person, and devoid of manifold characteristics.
"Great King!
This is called being endowed with three dharmas that enable one to attain the subtle and wondrous wisdom of a bodhisattva.
Great King!"
Furthermore, there are three dharmas that, when fully possessed, enable one not to become entangled in the snares of Māra.
What are these three?
First, it is said: toward all sentient beings, one does not give rise to anger and does not seek out their faults or shortcomings.
Second, to contemplate all sentient beings with equanimity, regarding them as fields of merit;

third, to be able to attain the contemplation of all phenomena as a single phenomenon—namely, that all phenomena are equal to space, being without action, without variety, without arising, without origination, and without cessation; that they are entirely empty according to their true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), and to practice the contemplation of non-apprehension through relinquishment.
"Great King!
These are called the three dharmas that, when fully possessed, cause a son of good family not to be caught in the snare of Māra and to be forever liberated from the path of Māra.

At that time, the chief consort of King Utpala, named Deva-Sundarī, together with eighty-four thousand palace attendants and maidservants, surrounded her on all sides as she proceeded to the place where the Tathāgata Candraprabha-gandhavijaya resided.
Having arrived, she scattered various kinds of flowers over that Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and praised him with these verses:
"The obscurations of afflictions are forever exhausted; O Unrivaled Honored One of Liberation and Virtue, how shall you instruct me to transform this female body?"
May I be endowed with the marks of a man, swiftly depart from all evil realms, and attain mastery over the Dharma with a supple mind.
O Supreme Sugata, Teacher of Gods and Men, who can grant the foremost benefit to the world—
having been granted by the World-Honored One the relinquishing of this female body, may I obtain the joy of tranquil extinction.
How can this man be described so swiftly?
He who tames himself and tames others for their benefit has escaped the pit of affection; he is peerless in the world, the most supreme.
Mindfully upholding this vast accumulation of merit, you are able to swiftly subdue all sentient beings;
may you now surely turn the wheel here, and we pray that you quickly open the path to the nectar of immortality.
At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata spoke these words:
"Good son! That Tathāgata Candraprabhā-gandhavijaya addressed the first wife of King Utpala, Sundarī, saying:"

“O Lady! You should rely upon and cultivate wise skillful means; you shall swiftly transform this female body planted in previous lives, until you reach Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and ultimate Nirvana, never again receiving such a body—except by your own vow.”
"O Noble Lady!
By what skillful means can the female karma planted over immeasurable past lives be swiftly exhausted without remainder?
O Noble Lady!"

There is the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, which establishes great undertakings, possesses great merit, and is capable of providing great protection; it skillfully extinguishes the evil conduct of the three karmas of the female body, causing all retributions of suffering to cease without remainder.

If there is a woman who hears this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī and recites it with a sincere heart, after exhausting this female form, she shall in her future birth obtain the body of a handsome man; all her physical parts shall be perfectly complete, she shall possess upright conduct and great eloquence, her actions of body, speech, and mind shall be harmonious and compliant, and she shall be able to cause all present and future enemies and detractors to completely disperse and retreat.

If there are various evil karmas of body and speech for which one should undergo bitter retribution in the present or the future, by the majestic spiritual power of hearing this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, the evil karma committed shall be extinguished in this very life without remainder;
this excludes those who have committed the five heinous crimes, slandered the true Dharma, or reviled the noble ones.

By the power of the majesty and virtue of hearing this sutra, when their physical bodies reach their end and they pass away, such offenses as these shall likewise be extinguished accordingly, leaving nothing behind.

If there are women whose karmic retribution for evil deeds committed through body and speech is as vast as Mount Sumeru, such that they would certainly undergo immeasurable suffering in future lives—then all such various seeds of karmic obstacles and residual retributions resulting from those various bitter fruits shall be extinguished without remainder through the power of hearing this sutra.

"Why is this so? Because all Buddhas of the past—Arhats, Samyak-saṃbuddhas—have spoken this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, and by receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, praising in their presence, extolling, and rejoicing in it, all the karmic retributions of suffering belonging to those sentient beings are entirely extinguished through the power of this sūtra, and the roots of goodness they have cultivated increase accordingly."

If the present Buddhas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in all the lands of the ten directions, for the sake of sentient beings, each in their respective directions, preach this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, those sentient beings who hear it will feel joy and delight; all their karmic obstructions will be eliminated without exception, and all the roots of goodness they have cultivated will cause them to flourish.

In future ages, in all the buddha-fields of the ten directions, wherever all the Buddhas preach this sutra, even those sentient beings who give rise to a heart of joy for but a single thought-moment shall all attain the end of suffering and increase their roots of goodness.

I, too, now preach this sutra; all who hear it should rejoice accordingly. Wherever the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, currently dwelling in the ten directions, preach this sutra, they shall together extol it and together rejoice in it.
“O Noble Lady!

If there should be a Kṣatriya king who has already received the royal seal and enters the territory of another land, and he obtains this Ratnaketudhāraṇī to write, uphold, and cherish it, then by the power of this sutra, that Kṣatriya king’s majesty and virtue will become lofty and far-reaching, and his great fame will pervade immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions. Even all the devas of the desire and form realms will hear the sound of his virtue, and all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth—along with immeasurable koṭis, nayutas, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Kṣatriya kings—will constantly follow him and together protect him.”

All strife, famine, hostile enemies from other regions, and the afflictions of wind, rain, cold, heat, and pestilence within that king’s realm shall be utterly extinguished. All malevolent spirits, yakṣas, rākṣasas, lions, elephants, and wolves will give rise to hearts of compassion; though they remain within his kingdom, they shall do no harm.

In that king’s realm, there shall likewise be no coarse, harsh, or bitter tastes; all painful sensations and afflictions caused by unpleasant touch will be extinguished; and all treasures, the five grains, fruits, medicinal herbs, flowers, and leaves will flourish and increase in their succulent flavors.

"If a consecrated Kṣatriya king, wishing to engage in battle against another Kṣatriya king of a hostile nation, should suspend this sutra upon the top of his own banner, by the power of this sutra, all the military forces of that enemy king will naturally retreat and disperse."

If those two Kṣatriya kings who have received the celestial seal should engage in battle together, and each suspends this sūtra atop a banner, then by the power of the sūtra, those two kings will immediately come to admire and love one another and reach a state of mutual harmony.
Thus, having accomplished immeasurable merit and bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to all kings of men, wherever this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī exists—

whether in cities, towns, or villages— neither humans nor non-humans, nor four-footed or many-footed venomous insects, shall be able to cause those who hear this sutra to suffer from disease, untimely death, or intentional affliction and disturbance.
Wherever this sutra may be located, one should exert every effort to arrange a great offering; one should welcome this sutra with all manner of offerings and place the scripture upon a lion throne.

Those who read this sutra and those who listen to it should, with a sincere mind, bathe themselves until pure, anoint their bodies with fragrant oil, and put on new, clean garments. They should observe the Brahma-conduct, scatter flowers of various colors, burn various famous incenses, and offer various delicious foods, reverently surrounding and making offerings to this sutra.

"If that person should encounter any suffering from illness, the calamity of untimely death, or signs of fear and evil omens, they shall all be extinguished and disappear through the power of this sutra."

If there are women who seek to obtain sons or daughters, they should all bathe and put on new, clean clothes, practice the pure life (brahmacarya), burn incense and scatter flowers, and reverently make offerings to this wondrous sutra; thus they shall give birth to sons and daughters endowed with merit and wisdom.

Such women, although not for their own sake, by the power of cultivation through the majesty and gravity of this sutra, after casting off this body, until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and even nirvāṇa, shall never again receive a female body;
except when they themselves make a vow to bring sentient beings to maturity.
"O Noble Lady!

Should a single verse, a single phrase, or even a single sound of this sutra reach the ears of anyone—down to the birds and beasts—those who hear this sutra shall likewise all be able to cast off their animal bodies, and shall cause all beings to swiftly attain non-retrogressive *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
“Good son! When that Tathāgata Candraprabhā-gandhavijaya of the past was preaching this sutra, he touched the earth with his right big toe, and this world shook in six ways.”
"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni’s preaching of this sutra now is likewise so, by the spiritual power of the Buddha.

At that time, the mountains, rivers, and great earth of this buddha-field shook in six ways, and immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, humans, non-humans, and others throughout the ten directions all gave rise to doubt and wonder.

A great light pervaded all buddha-fields, making the ground as level as the palm of a hand; Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains, the forests, and the walls were all hidden and no longer visible.

When the earth shook, those devas, nāgas, and yakṣas were first seized by doubt and wonder; yet, because they were empowered by the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata, the devas, nāgas, and others looked toward the four directions.

At a distance of one arrow-shot, they beheld Śākyamuni Tathāgata, and each was filled with joy and gave rise to a sense of rare wonder. Simultaneously, they joined their palms and gazed up at the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni spoke these words: “Good sons!

When the Tathāgata Candraprabhā-gandhavijaya preached this sūtra in the past, the earth shook in six ways as he touched it with his foot, and this buddha-field became as level as the surface of water. All devas and humans were filled with doubt and wonder; looking out in the four directions, they saw the Tathāgata Candraprabhā-gandhavijaya at a distance of one arrow-shot. Having seen him, they joined their palms and gave rise to a sense of rare wonder.”
"Good son! That Tathāgata Candraprabhā-gandhavijaya, for the sake of sentient beings, spoke this Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī mantra amidst the great assembly of devas and nāgas, saying: 'Tadyathā'..."
