“Svāhā, ninety-five. At that time, after the Tathāgata Śākyamuni had spoken this Ratnaketudhāraṇī, immediately thereafter, this great earth shook once again.
At that time, because those five hundred female attendants of the Māra-king had heard the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī,
their female forms were immediately transformed and they came to possess the marks of men; as did immeasurable asaṃkhyeya goddesses,
nāga girls, yakṣa girls, gandharva girls, asura girls, garuḍa girls, kinnara girls, and...
Nāga maidens, mahoraga maidens, and even all female spirits such as pretas,
piśācas, and kumbhāṇḍas— by hearing this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī— shall likewise transform their female forms and possess the marks of a man;
furthermore, they shall cause all virtuous sons to swiftly attain non-retrogression.
From Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi down to all women who are destined to receive female bodies in future lives,
their karma from past actions shall be extinguished through the power of this sutra.
At that time, all the women joined their palms together and prostrated with their heads at the feet of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, simultaneously raising their voices and speaking these words:
“Namo, namo! Homage to the rare one who is able to bring about unsurpassed benefit!”
Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!

We pray only that, out of great compassion, you will extensively explain this past event for our sake: why is it that we have now completely eliminated the physical marks of women and have fully attained and perfected the male body?

Filled with profound joy at this rare transformation, I have now resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this past event, so that immeasurable devas and humans may all attain the fruits of the Path.
At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata again addressed the noble son Bhadramukha, saying:

"In the past, when the Tathāgata Candraprabhā-gandhavijaya proclaimed the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī for Queen Deva-sundarī of King Utpala, Sundarī and her retinue of eighty-four thousand palace ladies and attendants had their female characteristics extinguished and male characteristics manifested. Furthermore, immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) goddesses of the various heavens, as well as all women among humans and non-humans, each transformed their female forms to possess male characteristics; even the karma for receiving female bodies in future lives was extinguished without remainder."

"At that time, King Utpala relinquished his sovereign position as a wheel-turning monarch and entrusted the four continents to the crown prince. He then, together with his consort Deva-sundarī, his one thousand sons, eighty-four thousand Deva-sundaras (which in the language of Tang means 'Heavenly Beloveds'), and ninety-two thousand other commoners, went before the Buddha Candraprabha-gandhavijaya. With faith, they abandoned the household life for the homeless state, shaving off their hair and beards and donning the dharma robes. Having gone forth, they applied themselves with courageous diligence, reciting, upholding, and delighting in mental tranquility."
At that time, those immeasurable koṭis, nayutas, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings all had this thought:
"For what reason has the Wheel-Turning Sage King left the household life to enter the Way?"

Those who were attached to the heterodox each said to one another: "This Fragrant Supreme Tathāgata delights in the works of Māra; he practices deceit and illusion. At times he transforms his female organs into the male form;

at times he shaves off his beard and hair and receives dyed robes; at times he speaks of rebirth in heaven for the sake of those seeking birth in heaven; at times he speaks of human affairs for the sake of those seeking birth among humans; at times he speaks of the affairs of animals for those born as animals; at times he speaks of the affairs of hungry ghosts for those born as hungry ghosts; at times he speaks of the affairs of hell for those born in hell; at times he preaches the Dharma of neither arising nor ceasing; or again, he illusorily manifests the body of a woman—his delight in the works of Māra is fully manifest in these matters."

That Candraprabha has assumed the appearance of a śramaṇa; I shall now certainly depart from this dwelling, for I cannot bear to see the form and features of that śramaṇa, nor do I wish to hear the words he utters.
At that time, among the assembly, the minister Kumāra gave rise to doubt and delusion, and spoke thus to the people of that country:

"All our wives, concubines, and handmaidens have been magically transformed by this śramaṇa; their female forms have been changed into male bodies, and they have all been transformed into those with shaven heads and dyed robes. I alone am left behind, escaping this in my state of grief."
"I shall now enter deep mountains and perilous valleys, places devoid of human presence, like a seer wandering to avoid demonic illusions.
All of you should remain in harmony with me and follow along; be careful not to enter the snares of that śramaṇa Māra."
"That base, illusory śramaṇa—I do not wish to hear his voice now, much less behold him with my own eyes.
When those ministers and citizens who had not yet attained realization heard these words, they all rejoiced.

When the minister Kumāra spoke these words, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of sentient beings all fell into the net of heterodoxy. Furthermore, he proclaimed false teachings to those beings, saying:
"There is no birth and death, nor is there liberation; whether one performs good or evil deeds, there will be no karmic retribution for them in the future."

This deceptive śramaṇa diligently practices the works of Māra; whether one goes to see him, pays him homage, or listens to his Dharma, it deludes and confuses the human mind. He merely desires to shave his head, leave the home life, and practice in cemeteries; he eats but a single meal a day, sustaining himself by begging; he delights in secluded places, enters his room, and speaks little; he is constantly weary of the five desires, music, song, and dance; he abandons flower garlands, ointments, and powdered incense used for adorning the body; nor does he take pleasure in various floral ornaments or in the indulgence of drunkenness and lust for the sake of gratifying the passions.

Yet that śramaṇa zealously delights in proclaiming the path of the snares of Māra; he is an enemy to all sentient beings. Originally, I had neither seen nor heard of such deeds performed by a śramaṇa, yet now he causes immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of sentient beings to see such signs as these. From the distant past until now, I have never before beheld such a person of evil views.

“Good son! Later, at another time, the great śramaṇa Utpala heard that the people of that country were fleeing to mountain valleys, or were themselves practicing evil paths, and furthermore, were teaching others to adhere to wrong views, disparaging the Three Jewels, and slandering the correct as being false. Having heard this, he reflected to himself:
‘If those sentient beings all fall into wrong views, failing to attain liberation and remaining in non-orthodox views, they will neither benefit nor be established in the Dharma.’”

I have become a śramaṇa; how may I cause those sentient beings who are blind and ignorant in future ages to leave the three evil realms and escape the snares of the four Māras, enabling those not yet liberated to attain liberation, and ultimately leading them to achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
At that time, having formed this thought, the Great Śramaṇa Utpala addressed the Tathāgata Candraprabhā-gandhavijaya, saying:

"For the sake of sentient beings, I have now aroused great valor and practiced great compassion; accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings surrounding me before and behind, I shall go to those borderlands, cities, towns, villages, and desolate mountains or treacherous places, to proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings."
If those sentient beings have fallen into wrong views, I shall now obstruct them and cause them to enter into right view, and even instruct them to abide securely in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Some may seek the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, or seek the vehicle of the Śrāvakas; some may be established in the fruits of sainthood, or be caused to go forth into homelessness; some may be exhorted to receive and uphold the Upāsaka precepts, or the eightfold fast-day precepts, or the practice of the three refuges; or for the sake of establishing all women so that they possess the male form and sever the karma of female organs, he preached this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī mantra.

Even as many as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings who have ever given rise to doubt or perversion toward the Tathāgata—all such persons attached to evil views—I shall obstruct and sever [their attachments] so that they may confess and reveal them.

Having given this instruction, he established them all in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and they all went forth from home together in the presence of the Buddha Candraprabha-gandheśvara to purely cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The man Kumāraśreṣṭhin had previously made this vow:
"That great śramaṇa is able to preach the art of illusion; he has destroyed my followers and seduced my kinsmen."

When you attain Buddhahood in a future age, I shall once again perform various demonic deeds against you—namely, at the time of your initial conception in the womb, during your childhood, during your youthful pleasures, at the time of your renunciation, and when you sit beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment.
"I shall afflict and disturb them in various ways and destroy them in various ways, causing them to fall away from the mind of bodhi. "Good son!

At that time, the Great Śramaṇa redoubled his diligent toil and, with courageous and vigorous perseverance, traveled through his native land; entering those mountain fastnesses, he spoke words of kindness and affection, using various parables to enlighten the people."

All those sentient beings beheld the Original King; hearing his preaching of the Dharma, they all gave rise to joy. They immediately turned away from their deviant minds and severed their former evil views, seeking refuge and repenting before the śramaṇa, and together they resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kumārabhṛtya and his followers, having subdued their evil minds and come to harbor right faith, made this vow:
"If you, Great Śramaṇa, who possess great compassion, shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a future age, we pray that you will deign to grant us the prediction of our own enlightenment."
"O sons of good family!
If you wish to know who that Universal Monarch Utpala was in the past, is he anyone else?
It is none other than my own self."
The king’s consort, Sundarī, was none other than the present Maitreya Bodhisattva.
The minister Kumāra, who slandered the True Dharma and harbored evil views, was none other than the present Māra, King of the Demons.

At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of sentient beings, having heard me preach the Dharma, collectively abandoned their wrong views and dwelt in the path of the Three Vehicles; they all attained renunciation, as did immeasurable women who became men through the power of the sutra—these are none other than the fourfold assembly among you here today.
“Good sons! You should now believe and accept my words; when you hear the account of the past life of King Utpala, do not give rise to doubt or confusion.”

Why is this? I recall that in the past, when the minister Kumāra saw his own retinue and countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings alike renounce the works of Māra, leave the household life for the sake of the Way within the Buddha-dharma, he conceived an evil thought, vowing: "In a future age, I shall raise an army of Māras to destroy your retinue, just as you have done today."

“Good sons! In the past, in the presence of the Tathāgata Candraprabhā-gandhavijaya, you gave rise to impure faith and uttered unwholesome words; through the retribution of such evil views, you deluded and ensnared sentient beings. Yet, by virtue of encountering the causal conditions of meeting a Buddha, you attained liberation. Due to the power of a single thought of goodness and your renunciation, from that time forth you have drawn near to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, making offerings and providing for them without weariness. In the presence of those Buddhas, you have made great vows and delighted in hearing the Dharma, even practicing the six pāramitās constantly.”

"Throughout the past, you have committed evil deeds with body, speech, and mind; for immeasurable kalpas, you have constantly dwelt within the three miserable realms, subjected to various sufferings and afflictions, and led by the obstruction of karma to be born within the paths of Māra."

Because I, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, have spoken this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, five hundred female musicians among that host of Māras immediately transformed their female bodies; simultaneously, they all attained the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Furthermore, immeasurable, incalculable, nayuta-hundreds-of-thousands of sentient beings, as well as the entire assembly of gods and humans in all worlds, all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieved non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable, incalculable, nayuta, and hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who all attained non-retrogression in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Chapter Three: The Submission of the Māra King. Chapter Three: The Submission of the Māra King.

At that time, when the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was preaching this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī Sūtra, he emitted a great radiance that shone everywhere throughout this Sahā world-system, illuminating all its hundreds of koṭis of four-continent regions with brilliant light.

At that time, throughout the hundred koṭis of realms here in the desire realm, all the Māras were stirred with alarm by the power of the Buddha. Beholding together the causes and conditions for the manifestation of this light, they all thought to themselves:
"This must certainly be the work of that evil Māra; possessing great majestic power over the four continents, he has manifested this light because of his great sovereign authority over us."
While he was reflecting thus, he perceived that the Evil Māra sat in his chamber of sorrow and affliction, feeling extreme dejection and resentment.
At that time, hundreds of koṭis of Māras from this world-system each abandoned their own palaces and came to the abode of the Evil Māra King of these four continents, saying:

"You, the Lord of the Desire Realm, possess great sovereignty; having emitted this radiance that universally illumines all things, for what reason do you sit in your chamber of sorrow and affliction?"
At that time, Māra immediately replied to all the māras present in the hundred koṭis of locations:

"You should know this: this śramaṇa born of the Śākya clan is the foremost in deceitful illusion. He has emitted this radiance that illuminates the world, causing universal agitation. All those in the world possessed of wisdom—Brahmā kings, nāga kings, yakṣa kings, asura kings, mahoraga kings, garuḍa kings, kiṃnara kings, and even other humans and non-humans—among whom there are wise and sagacious individuals, have all turned toward him and made offerings to him. Having sat alone in solitude for six years without a second companion, he has accomplished the power of the great illusion of signlessness."

By my own power, I have manifested supernatural feats, arraying a military host of thirty-six koṭis to surround me on all sides; yet though all the powers of Māra exerted great effort, they were ultimately unable to cause even a single hair of that Śūdra to tremble with fear, let alone be able to create further obstacles or disturb his seat of Dharma.

Now this Śūdra has achieved such an illusion of signlessness that his manifested deeds have shaken this great earth and routed my army, like felling a great tree where both root and branches fall together.

All realms of Māra were completely shrouded in darkness, yet at that place where he sat, a great radiance was accomplished. Having risen from his seat, he revealed and expounded [the Dharma] for the sake of all sentient beings; even the intelligence and wisdom of all sentient beings within these four continents were entirely pulled by the hook of illusion, such that I did not know their minds—where they were or what their destinies were.
When will they die? Where will they be reborn?
As for those among these six realms of existence who have taken refuge in him, I cannot even stir a single hair on their bodies, let alone cause them to waver in their faith.

"These five hundred exquisite female musicians, along with my twenty thousand sons and all their retinues, have all taken refuge in the śramaṇa Gautama and are sitting before him; today, I am unable to restrain them."

"You all now possess power, merit, and wisdom with mastery; you should assist me in taking the life of that Śākyaputra Śuddhodana, cause all sentient beings who have taken refuge in him to be utterly dispersed, subdue all the deceitful and illusory śramaṇas of the dark faction, and make our own white and pure faction of māras clearly manifest. From this point forward, you shall experience pleasant sensations."

At that time, there was a Māra named Prabhāsa who, observing this Jambudvīpa, beheld the body of the Tathāgata upon the Dharma-seat and heard his Brahma-voice preaching the Dharma with exquisite beauty. Having seen and heard this, his hair stood on end and he rose up in alarm, speaking these verses to that Māra-king:
"Among all the lands, this form is most supreme and extraordinary;
In merit and wisdom, he has long since purified his body."
Liberated from all afflictions, long associated with what is wholesome, liberated from all states of existence, you have exhausted every sorrow.
Do not be angry again now; there is no room for anger in one who has attained mastery.
Those who take refuge in this place have the foremost refuge in the three realms of existence.
If you should give rise to even a moment’s anger toward this place,
through that very delusion, you will bring about the destruction of your own happiness.
At that time, within the assembly, there was another Māra named Śaṇḍimika, who addressed the Māra King with these verses:
"By means of that great supernormal power and the marks of supreme merit, he is entirely without dependence; those who depend [upon him] shall proceed to liberation."
"Suffering is exhausted without remainder; he can preach the path to the exhaustion of suffering.
Even immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Māras cannot disturb or confuse him.
At that time, the Māra King spoke a verse in reply:
"All those who are now my sovereign subjects have completely submitted to Maheśvara;
before long, my realm will thus become empty. I shall have no place of refuge, nor anything left to attain."
At that time, within the assembly, there was another Māra named Navarajas who spoke these verses to the Māra King:
"The foremost power you previously possessed, And the deeds of your sovereign valor— Now you have lost that strength and are once more powerless; You cannot be compared to the All-Knowing One."
At that time, there was another Māra in the assembly named Kṣuracandra (Razor-Moon), who addressed the Māra King with these verses:
"Compassionate toward sentient beings, free from malice, Pure by nature and without dependence,
Liberated from the realms of the three worlds and wandering therein— He has no destination, no path, and none can harm him."
At that time, the Māra King replied in verse:
"All sentient beings within the realm of desire, Deluded, intoxicated, and with inverted minds, are attached to various desires;
They always follow and turn according to my will— How can you, together with me, not harm them?"
At that time, within the assembly, there was another Māra named Earth-Water (Pṛthivī-udaka) who addressed the Māra King with these verses:
"All existences are as unsubstantial as illusions or mirages; One who knows all existences severs all cravings.
Not clinging to existences, like space— How can one cause him distress?"
At that time, Māra spoke in verse, replying:
"Though he possesses mastery over the three realms, and constantly relies upon food, drink, and clothing,
and dwells in delight amidst the three types of sensation— how is it that death cannot harm him?"
At that time, within the assembly, there was another Māra named Tyāgaprema (Abandonment of Attachment) who addressed the Māra King with these verses:
"Whatever exists within the sphere of supernatural powers—whether it be evil Māras, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or others—none can touch the Buddha despite their various attempts to harass him.
How could you, as he approaches death, possibly harm him?"
At that time, the Māra King replied with a verse:
"In former days we cut off his food, rained down great stones from the midst of space, and uttered boundless insults in a hundred voices;
we sought to shake the very place upon which he relied."
At that time, there was another Māra in the assembly named Jñānacakṣus (Knowing Eye), who addressed the Māra King with these verses:
"When you were causing such turmoil at that time, did you see even the slightest trace of anger?
He looked upon you with a relaxed countenance, without frowning; he comforted you with gentle words, never with a harsh sound."
At that time, Māra replied with a verse:
"He possesses wisdom and is able to practice constant forbearance; He can sever the faults of craving and delusion.
With a heart of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, He gathers all that should be cultivated, leaving nothing uncollected."
At that time, there was another Māra in the assembly named Durjayanta (Difficult to Subdue), who addressed the Māra King with these verses:
“If the three fetters were able to bind him, we might indeed disturb and confuse him;
but since the Buddha has extinguished this net of delusion and its obstructions, how can you, at the point of death, hope to trouble him?”
At that time, the Māra King replied with a verse:
"Lend me your strength; prepare yourselves without negligence.
I shall transform the earth into water and bind the four mountains into a garland."
The void rains down great stones, and again releases clusters of iron sand;
with crescent-headed arrows, curved blades, and barbed darts, they hurl them so that his body is instantly shattered.
Thus, through diligent expedients, they cause him extreme distress and confusion.
"Join your efforts together, and the son of the Śākyas shall surely be reduced to ashes.
At that time, each of the māras spoke a verse; even among all the māras present in hundreds of koṭis of locations, their verses of inquiry and response were exactly like this.
At that time, all the māras in that assembly simultaneously raised their voices and spoke these words:
"In this manner, you should depart; each of you must adorn yourselves with armor in your respective palaces, and all the troops must likewise don their mail."

"May each of us employ the power of our supernatural faculties to manifest all manner of realms so that he may know them; though the śramaṇa Gautama be courageous and fierce, how could he withstand the vanguard of our military host?"

When these words were spoken, in that very instant, hundreds of koṭis of Māras from their respective abodes, each adorned with armor, led by individual armies of a thousand koṭis of followers clad in various armors and wielding various weapons, each separately prepared their chariots and descended into Jambudvīpa during the night. Arriving in Madhyadeśa, they each took their places in the air near the Buddha; even the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, and kumbhāṇḍas from the four continents likewise conceived faithless thoughts toward the Buddha and lacked any sense of reverence, and they likewise lacked faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Each of those Māras dispatched their own armies, adorned with various weapons and donning armor, gathering in great numbers at that place, desiring to harm the Tathāgata.

There was a seer named Prabhāsvāda who had mastered the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) and the sphere of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to an extent exceeding that of others; he constantly served Maheśvara and dwelt on the slopes of the Snow Mountains with a retinue of five hundred followers.
At that time, Māra immediately transformed his body into the likeness of Maheśvara and stood before the seer,
reciting these verses: “Born of the Gautama clan, Great Seer who relies on supernormal powers,
Wise one dwelling in Magadha, You now beg for alms in the city of Rājagṛha.”
"You should firm up your resolve and go to engage in various discussions;
having perfected the five supernormal powers, you shall attain definitive mastery.
At that time, after the Māra King had spoken this verse, he immediately vanished and returned to his own palace among his retinue, where he spoke these verses:
"Listen today to me as I speak; I have now attained incomparable knowledge.
Regarding that which is embraced and spoken by the Son of Śākya, I shall empower him with supernormal powers to bring it to completion."
He manifests his own realm through illusion, Overpowering the vast power of Mara;
Like a mother speaking gentle words to her child, He causes all disciples to give rise to joy.
At the first part of every day, he enters the city, Walking slowly while maintaining perfect dignified deportment.
Whatever desires my disciples practice or have abandoned, I myself shall seize and hold them.
I will manifest exquisite songs and dances before them, causing them to become deluded and attached upon seeing and hearing them.
Once my disciples have seen and heard these things and become deluded and attached, they will surely distress the mind of the Great Seer Śākyamuni.
At that time, another Māra within the assembly spoke these verses:
"I shall now manifest terrifying forms— Lions, camels, elephants, tigers, and water buffaloes—
Rushing swiftly toward that city, Startling all with a display of majesty and a voice like a thunderclap."
Through supernatural powers, they manifest immeasurable transformations, further appearing weapons before them;
those who have abandoned their various desires may at times be confounded and made to forget them.
At that time, another Māra from within the assembly spoke these verses:
"Now, at that crossroads, I shall conjure a multi-storied pavilion to stand before him;
with various strange forms and hideous faces, and wielding all manner of weapons, I shall intimidate and disturb him."
A great voice in the sky rained down swords and blades;
with the terrifying sound of thunder and hail, it caused one to lose mastery over that realm, swiftly causing it to vanish and no longer appear before them.
At that time, the Māra King, by means of his supernormal powers, arrayed his entire retinue and extensively manifested all the aforementioned states.

Due to the power of the Tathāgata’s great compassion and majestic virtue, he likewise extensively manifested various displays such as those. He immediately transformed this trichiliocosm Buddha-world so that its very substance became like adamant, which no demonic power could alter or shift. Furthermore, they were unable to produce evil sounds, nor could they create volcanic fires with fierce flames on all four sides, nor could they produce untimely black clouds or malevolent winds.
By the power of the Buddha’s sustaining grace, not even a single dragon was able to move its body to let fall so much as a single drop of rain.
At that time, during the first part of the day, the four great śrāvakas dressed themselves, took up their bowls, and entered the great city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.

At that time, as the Venerable Śāriputra was approaching the southern gate of the city, he encountered fifty māra youths. They were exceptionally handsome, adorned with exquisite beauty, and possessed the marks of a great man; they were walking along the street singing and dancing together. Seeing the Venerable Śāriputra coming from afar, they immediately stepped forward and took both of the Venerable’s hands, saying to him:
"Dance, śramaṇa!"
"You sing, śramaṇa!
Then Śāriputra said to the youth:
"You should listen attentively!"
"What you have never heard before, I shall now cause you to hear.
He then spoke these verses for the youth:
"The sense-bases are to be loathed; Like a slaughterhouse, they constantly deceive me."
Now that I have grown weary of them, I have reached the ultimate limit of their exhaustion;
the aggregates are things to be weary of, for they constantly deceive me like a place of execution.
Now that I have grown weary of them, I have reached the ultimate limit of those aggregates.
At that time, after Śāriputra had spoken these verses for the sake of the Māra youths, he then uttered this dhāraṇī:

“Tadyathā (1) vāhara (2) vāhara (3) vara (4) vara (5) mārīcivāha (6) satyavāha (7) amṛtavāha (8) svāhā (9). At that time, as Śāriputra spoke these verses and the dhāraṇī amidst the melodic tones, the fifty Māra youths and their attendants heard this sound of the Dharma; they attained what they had never experienced before and were filled with great joy. Their faith became pure, and they addressed Śāriputra with these verses:
“O Right Guide, we now repent; You who speak as a kinsman and benefactor to the world.”
"The aggregates are said to be fearsome; teach me how to leave them behind, so that I may constantly realize and see this.
When the Māra youth had spoken this verse, he prostrated with his head to the ground at the Venerable’s feet and sat together with him on the path to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, wishing to enter the great city of Rājagṛha for alms, saw fifty youths at the eastern gate of the city. Amidst their singing, they spoke this verse:
"All elements are to be weary of; The place of slaughter has always deceived me.
Now that I am weary of them, I shall reach the very limit of those elements."
All feelings are to be reviled; this place of slaughter has always deceived me.
Now that I have grown weary of them, I shall reach the very limit of those feelings.
Contemplating what is to be reviled, this place of slaughter has always deceived me.
Having grown weary of reflection, I have reached the limit of reflection;
all perceptions are to be loathed, for the slaughter-ground has always deceived me.
Now that I am weary of them, I have exhausted the very limits of those perceptions.
Then, having spoken these verses amidst the singing, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana further uttered this *dhāraṇī*:

*Tadyathā: 1. amaba 2. amaba 3. amaba 4. amaba 5. arāja 6. raṇajaha 7. śamkha 8. śamkha 9. śamkha 10. thagana-vama 11. svāhā 12.* At that time, as the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke these verses and the *dhāraṇī* for the Māra youths, fifty of the youths were filled with supreme joy and gave rise to pure faith, reciting these verses:
“Endowed with secret supernormal powers, The Noble Lord, Son of the Muni...”
The perils of the path of birth and death, The lamp of Dharma illuminates and reveals them all;
It can sever every fault and evil, Therefore I have given rise to faith and joy.
Now that I have taken refuge in the Buddha, I likewise take refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
At that time, fifty of Māra’s sons immediately prostrated at the feet of Mahāmaudgalyāyana in the middle of the street and sat before him in proper posture to listen to the Dharma.

At that time, the Elder Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra entered the city through the northern gate to beg for alms. As he proceeded through the streets, following the sound of the boy’s singing, he spoke these verses within the melody:
"All contacts are to be loathed; The place of slaughter has always deceived me.
I now weary of those contacts, And thus shall I reach the limit of all contact."
The sovereign lord of the sense-faculties, In the place of slaughter, always deceives me;
Now I am weary of this sovereignty, Therefore I shall exhaust its very limit.
Delusion and karma constantly cause transmigration, In the place of slaughter, they always deceive me.
I now weary of delusion and karma, having reached the limit of delusion and karma;
all states of existence are to be loathed, for this place of slaughter constantly deceives me.
I now weary of all states of existence, having reached the limit of all states of existence.
At that time, after Pūrṇa had spoken these verses for the sake of the Māra youths within the melody of song, he addressed the youths, saying:
"Human life is fleeting and difficult to preserve; it is like the rapid torrent of a mountain stream. Life is even more precarious than that, yet foolish worldlings do not perceive it at all."

Furthermore, young man! All ordinary worldlings are intoxicated by the wine of form and lack awareness; they are intoxicated by the wine of sound and lack awareness; they are intoxicated by the wine of fragrance and lack awareness; they are intoxicated by the wine of taste and lack awareness; they are intoxicated by the wine of touch and lack awareness.
Furthermore, young man! Human life is fleeting and swift, even more so than a mountain stream;

yet foolish worldlings neither see nor know this. They are intoxicated by the wine of dharmas and lack awareness; they are intoxicated by the wine of the aggregates (*skandha*) and lack awareness; they are intoxicated by the wine of the elements (*dhātu*) and lack awareness; they are intoxicated by the wine of food and sustenance and lack awareness; they are intoxicated by the wine of pleasure and lack awareness; they are intoxicated by the wine of birth and lack awareness; they are intoxicated by the wine of desire and lack awareness.
Furthermore, young man!

Human life is fleeting and swift, like the rapid torrent of a mountain stream; yet human life is even more transient than that. Foolish ordinary beings neither see nor understand this, remaining utterly unaware even as they are intoxicated by the wine of attachment to all sensory consciousnesses.
He then spoke this mantra for the young boy:

“Tadyathā (1) | Gāgapa (2) | Gāgapa (3) | Gāgapa (4) | Muntiṇi (5) | Avata (6) | Vavata (7) | Khavata (8) | Varma-artha (9) | Sthivata (10) | Svāhā (11). At that time, as the Elder Pūrṇa recited these verses and *dhāraṇī* phrases within the melody of song for the māra-boys, those fifty boys were filled with supreme joy and gave rise to pure faith, uttering these verses:
“You have now taught us the path of quiescence; The various realms are like illusions and mirages.”
"The world arises solely from conceptual construction; therefore, I dedicate my body and life to the Triple Gem.
At that time, fifty of Māra’s sons in the street immediately prostrated at Pūrṇa’s feet and sat before him in proper posture to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti entered the city of Rājagṛha through its western gate to beg for alms in successive order.

On the street, he encountered fifty youths of Māra, who were in the prime of their youth, possessed of exquisite beauty and upright countenances, and whose deportment was refined and dignified like that of sons of noble families; they were walking along the street singing and dancing together in play.
Upon seeing Subhūti, they immediately rushed toward him, each grasping the Venerable One by both hands and speaking thus:
"Sing, śramaṇa!"
"You dance, śramaṇa! Subhūti said:
"Listen attentively!"
"Young man!
That which you have never heard before in your previous songs, I shall now cause you to hear; for now, remain silent and listen to my singing.
Then, Subhūti spoke these verses for the young man:
"All conditioned phenomena, being of a fluctuating nature, are impermanent;
like illusions, bubbles, or mirages, though seen, they cannot be grasped.
These dharmas that arise and perish with such rapidity—only the wise truly understand them."
Contact and feeling are a burden of suffering; the deluded follow after them.
Conditioned things are oppressed by suffering, and all are entirely without self.
There is not a single wise one who can bring liberation from suffering.
Just as one has faith in the path to enlightenment, one should cultivate the single characteristic through close proximity:
namely, the relinquishing of all conceptualizations of phenomena, such as impurity and non-self.
All conditioned formations are associated with this; they are without reality and devoid of intrinsic nature or characteristics.
All phenomena are devoid of a life-principle or a nourisher; they have no self and no agent.
Abandon the deceitful mind of Māra and arouse pure faith toward awakening.
All consciousnesses arise based on their foundations, like lightning flashing within space.
Contact, sensation, volition, and selflessness—when observed, they are found to lack substantial reality.
This collection of ignorant, ordinary beings, these aggregates, perpetually flows on;
though pure minds arise through discrimination, no agent can be found.
The limit of reality is quiescent emptiness, capable of transcending all extremes;
this Dharma is free from ignorance, and thus the practice of Bodhi is taught.
Like a great master mariner, it universally carries all beings to enlightenment.
At that time, after the Elder Subhūti had spoken these verses for the sake of the māra-boys, he then uttered this dhāraṇī:

“Tadyathā (1) | Suvin (2) | Vivin (3) | Vinata (4) | Jakhin (5) | Cili (6) | Cili (7) | Cili (8) | Apacili (9) | Apahacili (10) | Tathatopacili (11) | Bhūtakoṭicili (12) | Svāhā (13). Then, as the Elder Subhūti spoke these verse lines and dhāraṇī phrases amidst the sound of song for the sake of these boys, those fifty boys were filled with supreme joy and gave rise to pure faith, reciting these verses:
"Relying on evil associates, I had not heard such a Dharma;
because of my folly and lack of wisdom, I committed this evil karma.
I now confess and repent; may the Honored One bear witness to me."
"Born from the Supreme Dharma, I therefore make this great vow:
may I attain Buddhahood and universally benefit the world.
At that time, the fifty youths immediately prostrated at the feet of Subhūti in the middle of the street and sat before him with proper decorum to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the World-Honored One manifested this street as being one hundred yojanas in extent, vast, magnificent, and pure.
Then Śāriputra sat facing north, Mahāmaudgalyāyana sat facing west, Pūrṇa sat facing south, and Subhūti sat facing east; the dwellings of these four men occupied half a yojana in total.

At that moment, within the ground where those four great śrāvakas were seated, a great lotus appeared, fifty cubits in length and breadth, equal in all dimensions. Its stem was made of Jambūnada gold, its petals of blue vaidūrya, its filaments of supreme treasure, and its pericarp of pearls. The fragrance of the flower was more exquisite than the scents of the heavens; such a lotus is born from supramundane roots of goodness.
From this lotus, a great radiance issued forth, universally illuminating the trichiliocosm; it rose up upon the streets above those flowers to a height of three human spans as a manifestation.
Even unto the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, this lotus appeared, manifesting at a height of five yojanas according to the measure of that heaven;
in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, this lotus appeared, manifesting at a height of one hundred yojanas according to the measure of that heaven.

This lotus appeared as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; manifesting with a height of half a yojana according to the measurements of those heavens, it proclaimed various exquisite phrases and meanings upon its petals. All the sentient beings of this earth and those gods heard these verses from within the flower:
"Only the Buddha is born pure in this realm, Having defeated that Māra and his hosts.
Because the Buddha is valiant, he turns the Wheel of Dharma; The world, for this reason, has no doubt."
Those who possess wisdom and understand the treatises, who know the Dharma, seek the Dharma, and seek liberation—
among all the wise people in the world, Upagupta is the most supreme.
Having been tamed by the Teacher, he skillfully expounds this sublime Great Dharma.
Supreme offerings in all the worlds, Offerings to the Muni, the Teacher who speaks;
Possessing wisdom of the three times, he teaches well, Able to reveal the Three Trainings to be learned;
He who can rescue the people of the world and the devas, Causing them to understand and know the immeasurable meanings of the Dharma.
Benefiting the world by teaching virtuous conduct, The lamp of skillful wisdom illuminates the world.
Skillfully expounding the sublime Dharma to sever the three stains, Wisdom benefits beings without weariness.
Causing those in the world’s extreme suffering to attain liberation, For all sentient beings shrouded in the darkness of ignorance,
Able to grant the unerring Dharma-eye, the entire great assembly has now gathered together.
Before long, this Buddha shall let out a lion’s roar; the Tathāgata can reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Endowed with wondrous form and power, he speaks in succession, seeing the world submerged in the great ocean of suffering.
Coming into this world, he beats the Dharma drum; dwelling in the protection of the six faculties, he abides in supreme protection.
These six are the wisdoms that follow along with the six supernormal powers—the supreme Dharma of the six perfections taught by the Buddha.
It is definitively taught that these six seeds are able to slay those dwelling in the village of the six sense faculties;
regarding the six unsurpassed matters upon which one should reflect, the Buddha, the Lord of Taming, causes them to be mindful.
Having spoken these verses within the lotus, he further addressed the various devas of the six heavens of the desire realm with these verses from within the lotus:
"You wander together in harmony, Delighting in and clinging to all desires;
Your minds are intoxicated by negligence, Enshrouded by the veil of craving."
Fools always delight in attachment, intoxicated by the wine of various desires;
because of such negligence, they do not make offerings to the Sugata.
All desires are impermanent and perishable, like the moon reflected in water.
The snare of birth and death is firm and strong; no sentient beings can escape it.
These beings have no refuge; attached to various desires through their indulgence in them, they shall never attain nirvāṇa because of their delight in those desires.
Constantly dwelling in a state of heedlessness, one is not in accord with cessation;
Failing to examine what was done before—whether pure or impure—one undergoes old age and death through karma; Fear constantly surrounds such a person.
Because of your negligence, you wander through the three evil realms.
By means of giving, discipline, and mental restraint, constantly cultivate heedfulness;
you should diligently protect and maintain the wholesome karma previously performed.
Reflecting on the relinquishing of desire and impurity, for the sake of attaining that which is difficult to find thereafter;
you should take refuge in the Sugata and listen to his exposition of the great meaning;
cultivate wisdom, which is the cause for liberation and nirvana.
"Corresponding with the Sublime Dharma, listen to such a great meaning.

Having spoken these verses within the lotus, [the voice] continued as far as the sixteen heavens of the Form Realm; remaining within the lotus, it further spoke these verses for the sake of the devas:
"Distinguish well the wholesome dharmas and practice them diligently; With a single mind, delight in dhyāna and remain free from clamor."
Tranquil and undisturbed, seeking liberation, one should sever hatred through the application of wisdom.
Regarding all thirteen kinds of self-conceptions, one should explain them through analytical discernment and cultivate supreme patience;
by this, one will ultimately and swiftly attain liberation, reaching the state of release from birth and death.
Those who crave and discriminate among the aggregates of form perceive the nature of the self as firm and tranquil;
yet they do not diminish the phenomena that arise, and through such views they wander in saṃsāra toward evil realms.
Contemplating that the three realms are eternally without self, unreal, devoid of intrinsic nature, empty, and unconditioned—
one cultivates patience through discernment in accordance with them, thereby attaining liberation from all states of existence.
They do not age, nor do they die of illness; they are free from meeting with the hateful and separated from evil realms.
All phenomena are equal to space; their practice is the non-dual cultivation of correspondence.
The path of ultimate purity is supreme; with a mind unattached, one purifies the sense faculties.
Just as the Son of Śakra subdued the four Māras, one should cultivate the single dharma-nature that is signless.
Free from all marks whatsoever, with disciplined conduct and the twofold abandonment—this path is taught as the supreme for them;
they cultivate the emptiness of all phenomena through discernment.
If one can discerningly cultivate this emptiness, There is no master, no agent, and no recipient;
Understanding that the nature of awakening is like space, One remains far removed from longing for the unsurpassed.

At that time, when the Tathāgata uttered these words and meanings of the Dharma from within this pure-colored lotus pedestal, all humans and non-humans in this world came together to the street and circumambulated the lotus seat; even the infinite and countless gods up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven all descended from their celestial palaces to circumambulate the lotus seat, gazing upon it and listening to the Dharma.

At that time, having heard this verse, the Māra looked all around and beheld the great city of Rājagṛha; he saw lotus flowers in the midst of the streets emitting this Dharma sound, as well as immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas of people sitting together around the lotus flowers listening to the Dharma.

Furthermore, he saw immeasurable, innumerable hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas of devas from the six heavens of the desire realm; all these devas had abandoned their palaces and sat surrounding the lotus flower to listen to the Dharma.

Having seen and heard this, he became even more overwhelmed than before; his mind was bound by intense grief, suffering, and remorse. His hair stood on end, his body trembled, and sweat poured from every pore. Running through the air, he called out to the other hosts of Māras with a loud voice, speaking these verses:
"Listen now, all of you! Restrain your external minds! I have no power of mastery over my own realm."
This is Śākyamuni, whose supreme and victorious power and vast practice of merit are spread throughout the world.
Causing those sentient beings to make their endeavors firm, he utters this sound of the Dharma from the center of a lotus pedestal.
The sons of gods and men have all come without exception; these resolute and virtuous ones all look up to you with longing thirst.
With single-minded devotion to the Sugata, they seek the path of nirvana—the supreme merit, the foremost and unsurpassed.
The deeds performed by the śramaṇa delude these three realms, bewildering all beings and leaving them with no other thought.
A great assembly of devas and humans surrounds the lotus;
swiftly raining down stones and making terrifying sounds, he goes forth with the fierce hosts of Māra to crush and destroy him.
At that time, another māra addressed the Māra King with these verses:
“Listen to our words; these words are for your benefit.
What dharma do you know, such that you do not restrain your mind?”
By the Tathāgata’s supreme power of retention, the armies of Māra have been utterly extinguished;
yet seeing the Sugata, our hearts are all greatly bewildered and distressed.
The Buddha is the Great Captain; his radiant countenance is supremely perfect and full.
"Having placed our trust in the Buddha as our virtuous refuge, there is no superior place of refuge elsewhere.
At that time, yet another māra stood before the Māra King, his entire body trembling, his face contorted with frowns, weeping and filled with extreme rage, and spoke this verse:
"You have lost the good path and dwell in an evil one; Can you not know the limits of your own power?"
You are without shame, comparable to our Teacher; the power of Māra has been extinguished by the Buddha’s might.
In this world, a gathering of lotuses, we listen to the Dharma with joy, purifying body and mind;
yet our defiled bodies have lost their vigor, and we do not depart to be extinguished even for a single moment.
"Now we all take refuge; we take refuge in the Muni-Indra.
At that time, there were further demons who all joined their palms toward the Demon King and spoke these verses:
"You have abandoned the practice of Dharma and delight in doing evil; the Buddha is our protector, the benefactor of the world."
Among all assemblies, the Buddha’s assembly is supreme; the Buddha has now come to this city.
We should go to him swiftly with pure eyes and a joyful heart, taking refuge in the one most honored in the three realms, the wondrous and excellent medicine for all sentient beings.
At that time, there was another māra in this void of space named Jñānaghoṣa, who addressed the Māra-king and spoke these verses in a loud voice:
"May you all be united in faith and joy; All of you, in harmony, listen to my words.
Resolve your minds and speech, abandon evil views, Bow your bodies, join your palms, and cast aside anger."
With a mind of awakening, one should maintain pure faith; rejoice in the Tathāgata’s supreme teaching.
Having taken refuge in the Buddha—a refuge so difficult to find—I shall today offer my faithful devotion.

At that time, immeasurable and boundless Māras descended from the sky in a single instant and arrived at the gate of the seven-jeweled city of Rājagṛha; each brought various kinds of adorned offerings and came to the place where the Buddha was, desiring to make offerings to the Bhagavān.
Some manifested as the form of a Cakravartin King; some manifested as the form of Brahmādeva;
some manifested as the form of Maheśvara; some manifested as the form of Īśvara; some manifested as the form of Nārāyaṇa;
some manifested as the form of Tuṣita; some manifested as the form of Jyotiṣprabha...
He manifested as an image of Śakra-devendra, or manifested as one of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
or manifested in the form of a youth, or manifested as an image of Vaiśravaṇa,
or manifested as Virūḍhaka, or manifested as Virūpākṣa, or [manifested] as...
Some transformed themselves into Dhṛtarāṣṭra; some transformed themselves into the forms of the ministers and attendants of the Four Heavenly Kings;
some transformed themselves into the form of the Sun Deva; some transformed themselves into the form of the Moon Deva;
some transformed themselves into the large and small forms of the stellar deities; and some transformed themselves into the likeness of asuras.
Some transformed themselves into the form of a garuḍa; some transformed themselves into the likeness of a kinnara;
some transformed themselves into the form of a mahoraga; some transformed themselves into the shape of a jewel mountain;
some transformed themselves into the shape of a mass of gold; some transformed themselves into various forms of jewels; some transformed themselves into [forms of] jewels...
As for the forms of these trees, some transform into the likeness of a kṣatriya; some transform into the forms of other non-Buddhist practitioners;
some transform into the form of the wheel-treasure (cakraratna); some transform into the form of the maṇi-jewel;
some transform into the form of the elephant-treasure, Airāvaṇa; and some transform into the form of the horse-treasure, Valāhaka.
As for the form of the horse-treasure, it may transform into the image of the woman-treasure, or transform into the minister-treasure of the treasury,
or transform into the minister-treasure of the military; in such various ways they each manifest transformations,
remaining before the Buddha for the sake of making offerings.
Some manifested blue complexions and blue bodies, adorned with white ornaments, each holding red parasols, banners, and pearl necklaces, standing in the air at the height of a *tāla* tree;
some manifested white complexions and white bodies, adorned with red ornaments, each holding yellow parasols, banners, and necklaces, abiding in the air;
and some manifested red complexions and red bodies, adorned with golden garments, each holding blue parasols and banners, standing in formation.
Some manifested red bodies of red hue, raining down white pearls;
some manifested white bodies of white hue, raining down red pearls;
and some manifested the appearance of celestial immortals, dwelling in the midst of space and raining down showers of flowers.
Some manifested in the form of śrāvakas, raining down various celestial incenses from the midst of the sky as an offering to the Buddha;
some manifested in the guise of gandharvas, playing celestial music;
and some manifested in the form of celestial maidens, sprinkling the ground with fragrant water from various precious vessels.
Some transformed themselves into the color of pure gold and black, burning various kinds of incense;
some transformed themselves into the images of devaputras, singing, rejoicing, and dancing;
some transformed themselves into various colors, joining their palms in reverence, gazing up at and praising the Tathāgata.
Some hosts of Māras, facing the direction of the Buddha, gazed upon him with single-minded devotion, each holding various kinds of maṇi jewels as offerings to the World-Honored One;

others, from the streets, palaces, pavilions, windows, gates, and turrets, from the four-tiered paths, the city walls, battlements, and watchtowers, from the spaces between doors, the trees, the multi-storied galleries, and the balustrades—each according to their respective dwelling place—joined their palms in reverence, gazing up at and making offerings to the Tathāgata.
The Ratnaketudhāraṇī Sūtra, Volume Three;
The Ratnaketudhāraṇī Sūtra, Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñāmitra of India during the Tang Dynasty.
The Remainder of the Chapter on the Submission of the Demon King:
At that time, the Demon King saw that all his demonic hosts, each with their own retinues, had taken refuge in the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Māra King became even more enraged than before; struck with terror and confusion, he raised his voice in mournful weeping and spoke these verses:
"I have lost my supreme majesty, And there is no longer anyone to aid me.
The Śramaṇa’s superior supernormal powers Have seized my realm of Māra."
One should further apply diligent skillful means, contemplating what must be done at a later time:
cut off the root of the lotus so that the multitude is scattered in all directions.
Once the lotus root is severed, cause the great assembly to fall into confusion.
"If the multitude has become confused, this shall be the power of my subsequent vow.

At that time, having spoken this verse, the Māra King descended from the sky like a swift wind, just as he had intended, reaching the street where the lotus had appeared. He immediately stepped forward, wishing to uproot the lotus; yet, by the power of the Buddha, he could not even touch it, let alone invade or pull it out.
Being unable to pull it out, he further desired to pluck the petals of that lotus flower; yet being unable to damage the pericarp, he then intended to raise his hand and strike the flower from afar.
At that time, the Māra King saw that the lotus was like lightning and like a shadow; although it was before his eyes, it could not be harmed or touched.

Then, the Māra King exhausted all his supernatural powers and performed whatever he could, yet he was ultimately unable to damage the lotus. Furthermore, wishing to terrify the entire great assembly, he immediately produced a loud, towering, and fearsome sound, but even this sound did not emerge.
Again manifesting his majestic ferocity, he raised both hands with great force, intending to strike the great earth so as to cause it to tremble.
At that time, the great earth was like empty space; it could not even be touched by hand, much less made to shake.
At that time, when the Māra King saw that this great earth could not be touched, he again had this thought:
"I shall now strike all the sentient beings in this great assembly so as to cause their minds to become disordered."
While he was thinking this, he did not see even a single sentient being who could be apprehended or touched, much less one who could be oppressed or coerced;
such was the manifestation produced by the power of the Buddha.

At that time, Māra’s distress increased even further; his entire body trembled like a tree in a great wind, and he wailed aloud with tears of grief and resentment, surveying the four directions as he spoke these verses:
“By the power of illusion, the śramaṇa Universally encompasses all worlds.
He has caused my mind to become dazed and intoxicated, Bewildering me in a single moment.”
The power of the merit of this realm is what belongs to me;
yet by means of illusory power, they have completely plundered it all.
Now that I have been cast out, I ought to return swiftly to my own palace.
"Even if I do not depart, it will further shorten my lifespan.
At that time, Māra wished to return to his palace; yet, despite forming this thought, he was unable to leave. His alarm and weeping intensified as he further thought:
"Has my supernatural power now reached its limit here?"
"Or is it through the power of Gautama's mastery?
Let me not have my life end before my enemies.
He then thought this again:
"I should now withdraw and go beyond this Sahā Buddha-field; I would rather die there than allow even a single sentient being in this Buddha-field to see me die."
While he was thinking this, he was unable to move even a single step from that spot, let alone disappear.
Immediately, he saw himself bound by five fetters; overcome with further terror and anger, he wailed aloud in grief and spoke again: "Alas!"
"You shall no longer see your beloved son or your various kinsmen.
At that time, there was a Māra named Jñānaghoṣa, who immediately transformed his body into the form of a Cakravartin King and spoke these verses to the Māra-king:
"Why is your mind so sorrowful? Why do you wail and give rise to such grief?"
The supreme among those in the world, the Tathāgata is the highest of the high.
The Buddha is fearless; one should swiftly seek refuge in him.
He protects all the worlds, like a lamp illuminating all realms of existence.
"Those who take refuge in the Protector shall ultimately be liberated from the three sufferings;
if one draws near to the Tathāgata, one shall attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
At that time, Māra the King thought to himself:
"If I were to employ that voice of wisdom, the śramaṇa Gautama should take refuge in me, and these bonds of mine would surely be liberated.
At that time, Māra, facing the direction of the Buddha, bowed with palms joined and spoke thus:
"Homage to the Unsurpassed Great Being among Men!"
“The Buddha is able to liberate those who suffer from old age, illness, and death;
I now take refuge in him. At that time, the Māra spoke in verse:
“This bondage is most perilous and greatly fearsome; I quickly take refuge, seeking the Sugata.”
Taking refuge in the Tathāgata brings liberation; today I take refuge for the first time in the foremost assembly.
Out of delusion and blindness, I harbored hatred toward the Perfectly Awakened One, and the transgressions I have committed are most extreme.
Now, relying upon your words, I repent; I place you before me to serve as my witness.

At that time, Māra, following those words of the virtuous man with wise voice, immediately took refuge in the World-Honored One before the Buddha; at that very moment, he saw for himself that his bodily bonds were liberated.

Having attained liberation, he further thought of returning to the palace where Māra dwells; immediately, he saw his own body once again bound by the five fetters, such that within this assembly there was no place for him to go, and he instantly returned once more to take refuge in the Tathāgata.
At the moment he gave rise to this thought, he immediately attained liberation once more in the presence of the Buddha.
When he formed the thought that he wished to depart, he saw himself bound; when he formed the thought that he wished to remain, he saw himself liberated.
In this manner, he was bound and liberated as many as seven times.
The Māra King, realizing that he was powerless to act, sat silently beside the Buddha. Chapter Four: The Great Assembly.

From the *Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, Chapter Four: The Great Assembly. At that time, those four great śrāvakas entered the great city of Rājagṛha to beg for food. They encountered the sons of Māra, who seized the hands of the śrāvakas and ran together through the streets, requesting the four sages to engage in unlawful singing and dancing.
At that time, amidst the sounds of song, the great śrāvakas preached verses concerning the path associated with nirvāṇa.

Then, in a single kṣaṇa, the great earth shook violently. Thereupon, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—who had previously attained pure faith within the Buddha’s teaching—shed tears from their eyes and spoke these verses:
“The Supreme Guide dwells in the world, yet within the Noble Teaching, evil portents have arisen.”
"By disgracing those śrāvakas before the eyes of the world, how can sentient beings give rise to pure faith?

At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, with tears streaming down their faces, went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived, they stood before the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"The holy teaching is manifest here; One should observe this day well."
"O wise ones, do not abandon it, for the sake of protecting the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"I shall now go myself to the abode of Māra, to cause the hosts of Māra’s army to be completely subdued."
"You shall become a guide for all the worlds, universally teaching them to head together toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the entire great assembly spoke with one voice, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Do not go! Do not go!

The Blessed One has previously declared that the Buddhas are inconceivable; the realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable; the realm of Māra is inconceivable; the realm of the nāgas is inconceivable; and karma, as well as the realm of karma, are inconceivable.
Among all such realms, the realm of the Buddha alone is supreme and unsurpassed.
We pray that the World-Honored One will not rise from this seat, but cause the immeasurable koṭis of nayutas of māra hosts to be naturally subdued.

Furthermore, they are able to reveal and teach immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of dharmas regarding the aggregates and elements; they exhaust the ocean of afflictions, destroy the web of false views, and enable immeasurable nayutas of sentient beings to enter the ocean of wisdom.
“World-Honored One!
Today is not the time to depart.
The Buddha said:
"Suppose all beings in the realm of sentient beings were to become entirely transformed into Māras, and even the entire great earth were reduced to fine dust.

If each of these individual particles were further transformed into a Māra, and all those Māras' powers sought to come and harm me, they would not be able to move even a single hair of mine, much less damage this body of mine."
Seated upon this seat, I am able to surpass immeasurable koṭis of nayutas of Māras and can likewise subdue them;
only these retinues of Māra remain difficult to subdue.
Nevertheless, I shall now go. Why is this?

This Māra has already manifested various kinds of ornamental offerings through his supernormal powers in Rājagṛha to honor me; out of compassion for him, I shall now accept them, so that this Māra’s mind may give rise to rare and supreme joy and produce pure faith, thereby planting the seeds of the roots of goodness for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, having spoken these words, the World-Honored One wished to rise from his seat.
Then the goddess who protected the Bamboo Grove, named Sundarī, approached the Buddha’s presence and, with tears streaming down her face, spoke this verse:
“World-Honored One, today is not the time for you to enter the city.”
This city is exceedingly vast, filled entirely with hosts of Māras.
Each and every one of these Māras harbors deep-seated malice in his heart;
together with billions of followers, they all desire to surround the World-Honored One.
The fires of their hatred are all ablaze, and their venomous minds grow increasingly deranged;
vying with one another to seize sharp weapons, they strive to vex and harm the Tathāgata.
I only pray that the Lion of the Śākyas will ultimately refrain from going.
"Or perhaps I shall meet an untimely death, and lose my great refuge.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer; he then rose from his Dharma-seat.
At that time, the guardian deity of the monastery named Dharanīdhara prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and spoke these verses:
“The great generals of Māra number five thousand; Each vies with the others to brandish sharp weapons.
With hearts harboring nothing but malice, they stand waiting for the Buddha; O Honored Muni, do not go this day.”
Having heard this, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer, as he was about to depart from the monastery.
At that time, there was a medicinal deity named Siddhimati, who prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and spoke in verse: “Alas!
The Dharma-boat is suddenly about to sink; the lamp of wisdom has abruptly ceased to shine.
The flavor of the Dharma in the world diminishes, while the thieves of affliction overflow.
Within all realms of existence, I possess not the slightest mastery.
The supreme Dharma is being destroyed; how can it be sustained?
Those hosts of Māra are vast in number, dwelling within evil dharmas;
each wielding sharp blades and weapons, they strive with poisonous intent to harm the Buddha.
"May the Sugata heed my words for the sake of benefiting the world;
I pray only that the Seer of Ten Powers, with his noble gait, does not enter the city.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One remained silent and gave no reply, as he was about to depart for the Kalandaka Grove.

At that time, within the great gate, there was a tree-deva named Dhṛtiśakti who, standing before the Buddha, wept with great compassion. Casting his body to the ground, he prostrated before the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"O Protector of the three realms of existence, you are about to lose your eyes; That which fulfills all desires is on the verge of being destroyed.
Swords and arrows in the sky are like venomous snakes, Seeking to harm the Buddha—please do not depart!"
When the World-Honored One had heard this, he remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the guardian deity of the great gate named Jyotiṣprabha raised his voice and wailed, prostrating with his head and face touching the ground at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke in verse:
“The renowned Great Brahmin within the city, Holding a moon-sword as a weapon, awaits the Buddha.”
"Two thousand of us harbor malice; we pray that you do not depart from this city.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not reply, as he proceeded toward the gate of Rājagṛha.

At that time, the guardian deity of the city gate named Tamālapatracandanagandhā raised her voice in lamentation from mid-air, rushed to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and spoke in verse:
“This path is surrounded by lions and elephants; With hearts of fierce valor, they strive to harm the Buddha, And to afflict the bhikṣus and create obstacles.
O Compassionate One, for the sake of devas and nāgas, I pray that you do not depart.”
Indra, the leader among the fourfold assembly, seeing that the Buddha’s teaching was about to perish, felt sorrow and suffering;
they gathered together in one place and, trembling with fear, said to one another:
"The Tathāgata is indeed the vanquisher of Māra, yet now Māra has transformed himself into a face of extreme evil."
Fearing that the Great Dharma will perish and worldly calamities will arise, the sun and moon lose their courses and the stars are obscured.
Beholding the appearance of these evil omens, they all strike their heads in grief, exclaiming: "How marvelous!"
The Eye of the Sun is scattered and destroyed, the Dharma-torch is extinguished; the True Awakening is trampled and the waters of the Dharma are exhausted.
The ruin of the world’s sublime Dharma is imminent, and the evil factions of Māra are gradually flourishing.
When the World-Honored One had heard this, he remained silent and did not answer.
The city-gate goddess, her admonitions to the Buddha having failed to turn him back, wept with flowing tears and spoke again in verse:
"O Muni, Honored One who surveys the world, The Supreme Speaker is about to depart to death."
Do not approach my city to meet with death and destruction; I am constantly reviled by the three realms.
O steadfast one, please listen to my words: do not perish within the city today.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, remain here to serve them, and liberate them from the fear of suffering.
Tathāgata, you should recall your original vow: to attain great bodhi and deliver sentient beings.
Countless beings are scorched by suffering; you are the supreme physician who brings peace to them.
To remain in the world for immeasurable koṭis of kalpas, for the sake of the multitude of ordinary people attached to desire—
"I shall teach the Dharma so that they may attain tranquility; this refers to entering into the meaning of the characteristic of intrinsic emptiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer, intending to enter the main gate.

Then the Earth Deity and the Great Flavor Deity, together with ten thousand deities of their own kind, both with hair disheveled on both sides of their faces, approached the Buddha’s dwelling. Standing with palms joined, they spoke these verses:
“Buddha, you recall your past practice of giving: You gave blood exceeding the four seas;
Your skulls were like the Iron Ring Mountains; Your eyes were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
And with various kinds of exquisite jewels, wives and children, elephants and horses,
clothing, food, and bedding, as well as whatever medicines are required for their ailments,
they perform the supreme offering.

Through frequent practice and extensive learning, you cultivated patience; Always filially supporting your parents, you performed difficult and arduous austerities to liberate suffering sentient beings.
According to the vows you made in the past, you have now attained Buddhahood and preach the supreme path.
Rescuing and delivering them from the ocean of worldly suffering, you preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings,
causing their suffering to be exhausted without remainder, leading them into the city of fearlessness,
and establishing them upon the path to Bodhi.
For those who have committed evil and lost the Way, Who repent for violating the precepts they heard,
May they fulfill their former vows And preach the Dharma for ten million eons;
Bathed with the waters of the eightfold precepts, May they cross over the river of afflictions.
Among all sentient beings in the three realms, there is none who is equal to the Buddha;
having himself attained liberation, he further liberates the world,
ferrying across all sentient beings within this ocean of the three realms of existence.
"Only the Buddha has attained such [realization], the supreme awakening in the world;
only the Buddha is the Father of the World. We pray that he will spread the Dharma of the Ambrosial Nectar.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had entered the city gate, in the space of a single kṣaṇa, there were immeasurable billions of nayutas of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the eight classes of spirits, who each shed tears in the void and spoke this verse:
"When I saw the Sugata of old, when he was taming the multitudes and bringing them peace,
preaching the Dharma for their benefit, there was no such affliction as this.
Yet the Great Teacher appeared in this evil age, spontaneously attaining great enlightenment."
He preaches the Dharma of the afflictive hindrances to bring the world to maturity, and thus he constantly lets out the lion’s roar.
Immeasurable evil Māras desire to extinguish such a Dharma; therefore, O Buddha, do not enter the city now.
Then, another deity spoke a verse, saying:
“The Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma, Abiding in one place for the benefit [of beings];
But now the Buddha goes everywhere— May none encounter evil.”
At that time, there were other devas who likewise spoke in verse:
“With compassion as your guide, Always acting for the benefit of sentient beings, Do not enter the city alone; As we see it, it will bring you harm.”

At that time, there were again immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, mahoragas, and others, whose faces rained tears as they descended from the void in a procession and stood before the Buddha.

There were immeasurable varieties of strange forms: some had disheveled hair, while others had cast off their necklaces; some had precious parasols, banners, and streamers all falling prostrate; some threw their entire bodies to the ground; some grasped the Buddha’s feet; some wailed with great lamentation; some raised both hands to beat their breasts in distress; some fell at the Buddha’s feet, leaping and weeping as they rolled upon the earth; some joined their palms before the Buddha to offer praise and prostrations; some scattered various kinds of exquisite flowers of diverse colors, powdered incense, ointments, flower garlands, kusha grass, silks, and other ornaments; and some scattered woven garments of precious materials, pearl necklaces, and various other rare objects.
Then the other hosts of devas, having made offerings to the Buddha, simultaneously raised their voices and spoke these verses:
“The austerities practiced by the Buddha Were for the benefit of the world.
Born in this age of decline, Do not abandon the multitude.”
The Buddha-work accomplished is not yet much; few gods and humans have attained realization.
By remaining long to reveal and teach the Dharma, you shall deliver the world of the three realms of existence.
Those who practice pure conduct will become vessels for the nectar of immortality.
One should arouse compassion for those to be taught, to rescue the world oppressed by suffering.
Within the wilderness of the six realms of existence, where beings lose the right path amidst birth and death,
one should show them the good way and teach the noble Dharma for liberation.
"This is most rare compassion: may the Great Awakened One abide long, turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, so that the world shall not be left without a protector.
At that time, another deva spoke again in verse:
"If the Guide should pass away, the world would be entirely blind and dark;
the Eightfold Noble Path and the three liberations would all cease to exist here.
We have already planted roots of goodness and remain heedful in our three karmas."
"Endowed with all requisites of bliss, He shall long abide as a treasury of merit.

At that time, there was again a host of Śuddhāvāsa devas who, together with their retinues numbering immeasurable, boundless billions of nayutas, gathered in one place. They spoke to one another in verse, saying:
"Do not be afraid; the Buddha does not decline. You should clearly realize this regarding the Great Awakened One."
I recall having personally seen the Buddha in the past; The koṭis of Māras belonging to the desire realm filled an area of thirty-six yojanas.
With sharp axes, keen swords, and blades and spears, They surged with fierce speed like rushing clouds; The hosts of Māras were valiant and fierce, their voices terrifying.
Upon reaching the Bodhi tree, they all fled in every direction; in a single kṣaṇa, they were all struck with terror.
How much more so now that your fruition is perfected and your fame is widespread—how could they possibly pose an obstacle?
At that time, other devas wept together and spoke in verse:
"In the past, a single Māra’s army lacked great power; Now there are ten billion, all possessing immense might.
They come to destroy the Tathāgata’s concentration—of this there is no doubt. If the Buddha should pass away, the world will be plunged into darkness."
At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the world-protecting devas prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and spoke in verse:
“With our limited wisdom, we entreated the Buddha to remain;
Out of compassion for our words, O Merciful One, Innumerable devas are now consumed by the fire of grief; For their sake, please let fall the rain of Dharma.”

At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed all the hosts of devas who had come together with his eyes of great compassion. Emitting a sublime Brahma-voice, he universally bestowed consolation and spoke in verse:
"Do not fear; now there is no cause for dread.
Though all the hosts of Māras come at once, They cannot harm or move me, Not even a single hair, much less my body."
I now comfort all beings, constantly preaching the sublime Dharma throughout the world;
for those who have thus lost their way, I shall extensively analyze and reveal the true path.
In the past, I have already performed deeds difficult to accomplish, Extensively bestowing food and drink upon sentient beings;
With dwellings and medical provisions never lacking, Who could today disturb or trouble me?
I may give away my carriages and elephants and horses, as well as my finely adorned precious ornaments;
even my slaves, cities, and villages—I am one whom no one can trouble or disturb.

Wives, concubines, sons, daughters, and all my kinsmen; the cherished and sovereign rank of the royal lineage—for the sake of benefiting myself and all sentient beings, why should my body now be destroyed?
My head, eyes, ears, and nose, my hands, feet, body, skin, and blood—I give even my life to sentient beings; who could then disturb or trouble me?
I have personally made offerings with my own hands to immeasurable koṭis of Buddhas.
Always delighting in precepts and much learning, who could scatter or destroy me?
Having performed immeasurable difficult deeds and being fully able to subdue the mind,
